parties:
Nurul Haque and others ------ appellants
Vs.
Abdus Salam Chowdhury and ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Short facts are that, one Abdus Salam Chowdhury, the predecessor-in-interest of the respondents, instituted Title Suit No. 80 of 1966 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Rangpur for establishment of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit property stating, inter alia, that he had some properties in the district of Jalpaiguri in India and also some shares in the Nipuchapur Tea Estate, Jalpaiguri. One Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers had properties in the Rangpur town as described in schedule A to the plaint. Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers were desirous of leaving this country for good and negotiated with the original plaintiff to exchange the property described in schedule A to the plaint with the plaintiff's properties situated at Jalpaiguri in India along with 30 shares of Nipuchapur Tea Estate described in schedule-B to the plaint. Thereafter, a deed of agreement was drawn up and signed by the parties in September, 1960 and in terms of the deed of agreement a deed of exchange was executed on behalf of Sudhir Kamal Sen and his co-sharers through their constituted attorney Abu Siddique Mazumder (defendant No.7) on 30-12-1960. The further case of the plaintiff was that Abu Siddique Mazumder was friendly with the plaintiff from before and since the plaintiff could not come to Rangpur from India at the relevant time for the purpose and since he had none to look after his properties the plaintiff appointed Abu Siddique Mazumder (defendant No.7) as his attorney by a power of attorney dated 21-1-1961 to manage and look after his property at Rangpur. It was also the case of the original plaintiff that at the time of exchange the property in suit was under requisition of the Government and occupied by the Manager, Employment Exchange, Rangpur, Thana Agriculture Officer, Rangpur and one Ashraf Hussain. Thereafter, on 2-9-1961 the property was de- requisitioned and he got vacant possession with respect to a portion described in schedule-C to the plaint and allowed the remaining portion of schedule-A property to be in possession of the said Agricultural Officer as a tenant under him and in this way the plaintiff became absolute owner of schedule-A property by exchange. The plaintiff asserted that he allowed his attorney Salamatullah who is defendant No. 6 to occupy and reside in a portion of the property described in schedule-C on behalf of the plaintiff as his licensee on condition that he would vacate the premises when demanded by the plaintiff. The plaintiff thereafter permanently left India and came to live in the then East Pakistan on 25-3-1961 and on his demand said Salamatullah promised to leave the disputed property soon. In April, 1962 Salamatullah was transferred to Karachi but he left for Karachi without handing over possession to the plaintiff. The plaintiff further asserted that defendant Nos. 1-5 illegally entered into the premises as described in schedule-C without any knowledge of the plaintiff. The original plaintiff mutated his name with the Municipality and has been paying rent to the Government after duly registering his name in the Govt. records and he revoked the power of attorney earlier granted in favour of defendant No. 6 as he found that his interest at the hands of his attorney was not safe. Thereafter, the original defendant No. 1 claimed the property in suit asserting the original plaintiff as his benamder and hence the suit. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1-5 and 7 contested the suit by filing written statement and their case, in a nut shell, is that defendant No. 1 is the father of defendant Nos. 2-4 and defendant No.1 used to live at Jalpaiguri in India and was connected with several Tea Estates and in 1951 he became the Secretary of Rahimia Lands and Tea Company (Private) Ltd which was a concern of Nawab Mosharraf Hossain's family and the original plaintiff went to Jalpaiguri from Noakhali immediately after partition of India and when he was in difficulty he sought help from original defendant No.1 and was appointed a Munshi in the Longarkhana of the Nawab family where the defendant No. 1 used to reside and he earned confidence of defendant No.1. The further case of the original defendant No. 1 is that sometime after partition of the Sub-Continent, the defendant No.1 sent his son, who is defendant No.2, in January, 1951 to Rangpur and when he himself was living at Jalpaiguri at that time. He was subsequently transferred to Calcutta office of the Rahimia Land and Tea Company (Private) Ltd and at that time he came in contact with the owners of the suit property and they agreed to exchange the same with the property of the defendant No. 1 in India and for expediency defendant No. 1 made the plaintiff his benamder as he was a man of defendant's confidence and the exchange deed was finalised accordingly and prayer was made for de-requisition of the property in the name of the plaintiff who is the benamder of defendant No.1. The further case was that there was no negotiation with Satish Kamal Sen for the exchange of the property with the plaintiff who is only a benamder of defendant No.1 in relation to the disputed property. The further case is that defendant No. 1 is the real and beneficial owner of the suit property and the same was never possessed by defendant No. 6 on behalf of the plaintiff as a licensee. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is not a proper judgment of reversal inasmuch as it does not conform to the long established principle that in reversing the judgment of the trial Court the appellate Court must fully apply its judicial mind to each and every finding of the trial Court and the decision based and the reasons given therefor and those findings and reasoning are required to be set aside with cogent reasons but these well established principles of dispensation of even handed justice have been glaringly violated in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division to the great prejudice of the appellants resulting in miscarriage of justice and further submission that the High Court Division committed illegality in deciding the case in a causal and indifferent manner as the impugned judgment ex facie bears ample testimony of non-application of judicial mind by the High Court Division to the most relevant issues in the case and the findings arrived at by the trial Court and the further submission that while interfering with the judgment of the trial Court the High Court Division failed to notice that the trial Court's judgment was based on totality of the factual findings on the relevant issues of facts that normally crop up as pertinent questions in a case of benami transaction and not a single issue in isolation and also the submission that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), was not aware of the legal position as to on whom lay the onus of proof in a case of benami transaction though with little care could have found that the trial Court was quite conscious with regard to the onus of proof in benami transaction, and the further submission that the High Court Division failed to appreciate the long established principle, criteria and factors pertaining to benami transaction such as motive for the benami, how and by whom the consideration was paid, the conduct of parties both during and after the transaction, custody of the title deeds possession of the property, negotiated deal and various other matters connected with the transaction and held that original defendant No. 1 successfully discharged the onus that lay on him and established that he was the real and beneficial owner of the property in suit and that the original plaintiff was his benamder with respect thereto and the further submission that the High Court Division ought to have discussed the elaborate evidence relating to the topic of custody of the basic documents but has not applied its Judicial mind in this regard, and the further submission that the High Court Division it appears tried to say that in a benami transaction only possession of the title deed is the main criteria which is not at all correct and the submission that the High Court Division in this case though is a final Court of fact discarded the judgment of the trial Court and its finding in a very superficial and summary fashion in one sentence stating that the defendant failed to discharge his onus regarding exchange and such hasty and abrupt procedure can hardly be countenanced by the Appellate Division which would upset the whole jurisprudence as to the judicial duties and obligations of the appellate Court and negation of justice, and the further submission that the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) had the advantage of observing the demean our of the witnesses and, as a matter of fact, assessed the credibility and reliability of DW 3 Mahtabuddin Khan, Advocate who drafted the exchange deed at Rangpur and relying on his testimony along with other reliable evidences held that the basic document of title was with defendant No. 1 when the same was shown to DW 3 a few days before September, 1965 lndo-Pak War and the said document was handed over to the plaintiff while a boundary dispute arose. But the High Court Division failed to appreciate this aspect of the matter and also the evidence of DW 3 which has caused miscarriage of justice. 

 7. The case of the plaintiff was that he was the real owner of the disputed property and purchased the same with own money and for his own benefit, whereas the case of the defendant No.1 was that the plaintiff was his benamder and the defendant No. 1 purchased the suit property with his own money and for his own benefit. The vital point for consideration in this case is whether the plaintiff was the real owner or he was the benamder of defendant No.1, in respect of the disputed 'A' schedule property situated in the centre of Rangpur town. The deed of agreement Exhibit 3 dated 1-9-1960 was executed by admitted owners of disputed property Satyabati Devi, Sudhir Kamal Sen and other co-sharers in Calcutta in favour of the plaintiff Abdus Salam Chowdhury as well as the deed of exchange Exhibit 1 executed by defendant No. 7 Abu Siddique at Rangpur on 31-12-1960 on the basis of the power of attorney, Exhibit 2 dated 5-9-1960 executed by Satyabati Devi and her co-sharers in Calcutta regarding the suit property were by the original plaintiff from his custody. 

 9. The trial Court observed that in the circumstances of the case the onus, rather heavy onus, lies on the defendant No. 1 to establish his assertion that the plaintiff was his benamder in respect of the disputed property. The trial Court further held that in all cases of benami transaction it is necessary to consider the motive for benami, how and by whom the consideration was paid, the conduct of the parties both during and after of the transaction, custody of the title deeds, possession of the property and various other matters connected with the transaction. 

 16. It is on record that in respect of Kusumalaya, Kusum Kamini executed the power of attorney in favour of elder brother's son of the defendant No. 1 and the case of the defendant No.1 is that his son defendant No.2 bore all expenses in respect of execution of document for Kusumalaya in favour of the plaintiff under his instruction. It is in the evidence of plaintiff that he received the original document in respect of Kusumalaya from his attorney, Lutfor Rahman, elder brother's son of defendant No.1. 

 18. Exhibit 2 is the power of attorney executed by Sudhir Kamal Sen and others in respect of the disputed property. In this power of attorney defendant No.6 Abu Siddique Majumder, brother-in-law of defendant No. 1 was appointed on 5-9- 1960 as a constituted attorney for doing the needful in the matter. It is undisputed that Abu Siddique Majumder is not related to the plaintiff nor a close man of the plaintiff. Exhibit 2(b) is another general power of attorney executed on 25-1-1961 by plaintiff Abdus Salam in favour of Abu Siddique Majumder, brother-in-law and Salamatullah, full brother of defendant No. 1 in respect of disputed property and other properties. It is to be noticed that normally the plaintiff is supposed to appoint his close relation as attorney by the power of attorney relating to the disputed property. But he appointed the close relations of the defendant No. 1 as attorneys. The learned Advocate for the appellants argued that this goes to show that, in fact, the close relations of defendant No. 1 were appointed as attorneys as the defendant No. 1 was the real owner and the plaintiff was benamder. The trial Court held that the plaintiff did not adcillce any evidence to corroborate him regarding tlie transaction but the defendant No.1, on the other hand, examined DW 9 (defendant No.2), the constituted attorneys DWs 2 & 5 of the plaintiff in respect of the disputed property and DW 3 Mahatabuddin Khan, a Senior Advocate of Rangpur Bar and Vice-Chairman of Rangpur Pourashava and DW 8 Ashraf Hossain who admittedly, occupied a portion of the disputed property at the relevant time and gave initial information to the defendant No. 1 regarding intention of the owners of the disputed property to sell the same. These witnesses corroborated him regarding the transaction and custody of the original documents. 

 19. We have also noticed that DWs 2 and 5, Salamatullah and Abu Siddique Majumder respectively constituted attorneys of the plaintiff in respect of the disputed property and DWs 3,6, 8, 9 in their evidence supported the 'Case of defendant No. 1 and, in our view, their evidences, especially the evidence of DW 3, were rightly taken into consideration by the trial Court regarding custody of the original documents by the defendant No. 1. The trial Court gave importance to the evidence of DW 3 Mahatabuddin Khan, a Senior Advocate practicing in the civil side at Rangpur Bar and Vice-Chairman of Rangpur Municipality since 1939. He joined the Bar on 7th August, 1925. He stated that he drafted the deed of exchange Exhibit 1 at the instance of DW 2 Salamatullah and DW 5 Abu Siddique, full brother and brother-in-law respectively of the defendant No. 1 regarding the house in suit. He further stated that power of attorney and agreement executed in Calcutta were placed before him in connection with .preparation of the draft and DW 2 Salamatullah told him that his brother (defendant No.1) was purchasing the house in suit in the name of the plaintiff. He further stated that long after that the deed of exchange was shown to him by defendant No.1, Nurul Haque and Abu Siddique. He further stated that defendant No. 1 pointed out some mistakes in the number of some shares as written in the deed of exchange and this meeting with defendant No.1. Nurul Haque, took place few days before September War of 1965. He saw the deed of exchange and other documents Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 with Nurul Haque, defendant No. 1, on that occasion. The defendant's case is that when boundary dispute arose with Dr T Rahman he handed over original title deeds to the plaintiff to file a case through Mr Taleb Ali, Advocate. We have also gone through the evidence of DWs 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 9. We are of the view that the trial Court has rightly placed reliance on their evidence, and specially the evidence of DW 3, and, in our view, the plaintiff could not dislodge the evidence of DW 3 regarding the custody of the original documents by the defendant No. 1 till the boundary dispute with Dr T Rahman when those were handed over to the plaintiffs. 

 23. The defendant No.1, Nurul Haque as DW 1 in his evidence stated that at the time of agreement Exhibit 3 dated 1-9-1967, Satyabati and others handed over some papers including three dakhilas to him and he filed those dakhilas on 10-5-1967 i.e. few days after the filing of the written statement before the trial Court, and those three dakhilas were marked Exhibit P, P(1) and P(2). The three dakhilas relating to payment of rent for the year 1363 BS to the Government Acquired Estate are in respect of the disputed property. The plaintiff did not give any satisfactory explanation as to how these dakhilas went to the custody of the defendant No.1. The normal presumption is that those were handed over to the defendant No. 1 by the original owners at the time of negotiation of the transaction. 

 26. It is an admitted case of both parties that an amount of Taka 10,000 was in deposit as compensation of the disputed property for the period of requisition and the plaintiff withdrew the entire amount from the requisition department sometime after his arrival at Rangpur from Jalpaiguri. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record arrived at the conclusion that the withdrawal of this amount from the office of Deputy Commissioner by the plaintiff does not prove anything conclusively or that he is the real owner of the property. The trial Court also held that since the title deeds stood in the name of the plaintiff, it was rather natural that he would withdraw the amount. In our view, the above findings of the trial Court are based on the materials on record. 

 27. The plaintiff's case is that he got delivery of the deed of exchange (Exhibit 1) from scribe Bazlur Rahman after his arrival at Rangpur. The case of the defendant, on the other hand, is that the receipt of the document was with Abu Siddique (DW 5) who executed the same as constituted attorney of the plaintiff and he endorsed the same to the scribe and got back the original document from the scribe and kept the same in his custody and later on handed over to defendant No. 1. It is undisputed that at the time of execution and registration of the document plaintiff was not at Rangpur and he came to Rangpur afterwards. The trial Court accordingly, concluded that the plaintiff was not known to scribe, Bazlur Rahman from before and, as such, unless the plaintiff was introduced to the scribe by DW 6 Abu Siddique the scribe was not supposed to hand over the original document to a stranger and this fact belies plaintiff's story that he got delivery of the original deed of exchange from the scribe. The defendant's case that Abu Siddique, who as attorney executed the deed, got delivery of the same and kept in his possession and later on handed over to the defendant No.1 appears to be probable. 

 28. It is on record that the plaintiff filed a criminal case on 10-5-1966 against defendant No. 1 and others. The trial Court found that only after getting possession of the original title deeds the plaintiff filed the criminal case and the present suit against the defendant No. 1 and others. 

 29. Therefore, from our above discussion, it is clear that the trial Court meticulously considered the evidences both oral and documentary, the facts and circumstances of the case and all other relevant aspects and then came to the conclusion that the defendant No. 1 having sufficient means acquired the disputed property with his own money and for his own benefit in the benami of the plaintiff, his trusted man and the defendant No. 1 was in possession of the original deeds and only in May, 1966 when trouble arose with neighbor Dr T Rahman regarding boundary, the defendant No. 1 handed over the title deeds to the plaintiff to file an application before the Deputy Commissioner through Mr Taleb Ali, Advocate and getting possession of the original title deed the plaintiff got his name mutated on 27-5-1966 in respect of disputed property.

parties:
President, Coronation Hall Committee and DC, Khulna ----- Petitioner Defendant-Appellant
Vs.
Executive Committee, Khulna and others ----- Opposite Parties Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Rezaul Hasan, J: This Rule under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) has been issued at the instance of the Defendant- Appellant calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and decree dated 03-9-2006 of the Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna passed in Title Appeal No. 177 of 2005 and affirming that dated 08-6-2005 of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Suit No. 49 of 2002 should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Relevant facts for the disposal of this rule, in brief, are that, Khulna Naitto Nikatan represented by its Executive Committee (18 members in all), herein after referred to as the plaintiffs, has filed Title Suit No. 49 of 2002 before the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna with following prayers, namely- 

 in respect of the property described in the schedule to the plaint. The basis for claiming title in the suit land, being 0.28 acres of land under CS Plot No.45/117 under CS Khatian No. 473/1 corresponding to SA Plot No. 169 under SA Khatian No.7 of Mouja Helatola, Police Station and District Khulna, is that the suit land was gifted by the then Hindu Jaminder in favour of the plaintiff at the request of some cultural minded people of the locality. In support of the plaintiffs case, it has examined four persons as witnesses. It has also adduced and proved certain documents before the trial Court which were marked as Exhibits-1 to 13. 

 4. The trial Court after hearing the parties, represented by their respective Advocates, by its judgment and decree dated 08-6-2005 (decree signed on 10-9-2005) has allowed the suit declaring that the plaintiff has title, ownership and authority in respect of 0.28 acres of suit land including the Coronation Hall and other establishments built thereupon. 

 5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court the defendant preferred an appeal, numbered as Title Appeal No. 177 of 2005, challenging the legality of the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 8. Mr. Mosharraf Hossain Sarder, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the petitioner along with Mrs. Shahida Begum and Mr. Khondaker Moderesh Elahi, learned Assistant Attorneys General having placed the application for revision and drawn our attention to the materials on record, firstly submits that in this particular case the Court of appeal has not independently assessed the evidence on record for itself as the last Court of facts and without reading the evidence properly interpreting the evidence adduced in the case, has erroneously affirmed the judgment and the, decree passed by the Court below. Besides the appellate Court has also failed to appreciate and apply the principles of law decided by the Supreme Court and cited before him at the time of hearing argument. He next submits that, the trial Court although recorded that neither of the parties to the suit has been able to prove original title in the suit land and that the plaintiff has failed to prove the alleged gift made in their favour by the then zaminders. It has, however, decreed the suit without appreciating the settled legal position that the onus lie on the plaintiff to prove its case and that the plaintiff cannot succeed on basis of the weakness or lacuna in the defence case. He next submits that, the trial Court has passed the decree stating as reason that even if for arguments sake it is considered that the plaintiff has failed to prove the fact of acquiring title on the basis of any gift, then it has at least acquired title by virtue of adverse possession, whereas the settled law is that adverse possession cannot be the basis of claiming title, nor it was the case of the plaintiff that it has acquired title in the suit land by virtue of adverse possession and, as such, the impugned judgment and decree has been passed erroneously as well as based on a third case, not to be found in the pleadings. He then submits that the Court below ought to have noticed that in the CS and SA Khatian (Exhibit Umma and Umma-1) name of the defendant has been recorded as owner as well as the land development tax receipt (খাজনা দাখিলা), Exhibit-4 series, also prove payment of Khazna in the name of the defendant. Exhibit-2 SA Khatian No. 7 and the Khazna Dhakila prove possession and ownership of the defendant in the suit land as well as in the establishments built there- upon. He also submits that the two agreements, marked as Exhibit-9 series, also proved that the Coronation Hall was let out to the Society Cinema Hall by the defendant as land lord. These evidences also proved title and ownership of the defendant in the suit properties, which both Courts below have failed to read, to interpret and to appreciate. Finally he submits that, the schedule of the plaint is vague and the suit property cannot be identified with reference to the schedule. Hence on this ground also the suit ought to have been dismissed. He concludes submitting that, the suit has been filed by the plaintiff in anticipation of litigation for their failure to render accounts as to the income and expenditure of the plaintiff organization which was receiving donation from the defendant at the rate of 40% of the rental income and the defendant had authority to ask for rendering accounts by the plaintiff organization. Accordingly, the learned Advocate maintained that, in passing the impugned judgment and decree the appellate Court has committed error of the law and that has resulted in error in the impugned judgment and decree occasioning failure of justice, so the impugned judgments and decrees are liable to be set-aside and the suit be dismissed. In support of his contentions the learned Deputy Attorney General has referred to that cases Abdul Kader vs Abdullah, reported in 51 DLR 435; Noor Mohammad Khan vs Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR 435; Kamal Baksh vs Siraj Bakshi, reported in 7 BLT (AD) 329 and Bangladesh vs Abdul Hye, reported in 56 DLR (AD) 53. 

 9. The learned Advocates Mr. M Kamrul Hoque Siddique appearing along with Mr. AKM Alamgir Parvez Bhuiyan, appearing on behalf of the defendant-opposite parties, on the other hand, referring to the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 (SR Act) submits that the prayer made in the plaint and as allowed by the Courts below is well within the ambit of the provisions of section 42 of the SR Act in as much as the plaintiff has been occupying some establishments built on suit property and has been receiving a portion of the rental income of the suit property and that these rights as well as the title of the plaintiff has been lawfully declared in favour of the plaintiff. He has also submitted that the utility bills were being paid by the plaintiff and that clearly shows that the plain- tiff is in occupation of the suit property. Accordingly, he submits that in passing the impugned judgment and decree the Courts below have committed no error of law resulting in any error in the decisions occasioning failure of justice. He therefore prayed for discharging in the rule. The learned Advocate, in support of his contention, has referred to the following decisions Aminul Islam vs Kilburn & Co. Ltd. Pakistan, reported in 18 DLR 691; Jinnat Ali Mukhtear vs Abdul Majid, reported in 27 DLR 385; Irfan Ali vs Joynal Abedin Miah (Late), reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216; AI-haj Ahmed Hossain Khan vs Rezaur Rahman, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 225; Noor Mohammad Khan vs Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR 436; Moinuddin Ahmed alias Farooq vs Khusheda Begum, reported in 54 DLR 354; Shishir Kanti Pal vs Nur Md reported in 54 DLR 440 and Md. Banazir Ahmed Vol" Debendra Chandra Saha reported in 4 BLT (AD) 150. 

 14. However, our perusal of the judgment of the appellate Court also reveals that the appellate Court has also recorded that none of the parties has adduced any document as to the original title in respect of the suit land and both the Courts below have recorded that the plaintiff has failed to prove the fact of gift on the basis of which it has claimed its ownership and title in the suit land. However, on perusal of the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the trial Court has decreed the suit for the reason that the plaintiffs were entitled to get the decree at least on the basis of the adverse possession since long as it has recorded in its judgment dated 08-6-2005 that- 

 15. Having perused plaint, we find that the plaintiff has not claimed declaration of its title or ownership or possession in the suit properties based on any adverse possession. Rather, their specific case-was that, at the request of some dignitaries and cultural minded people of the locality the then Hindu Zaminder has gifted the property in favour of the plaintiff, but both the Court below have recorded that the plaintiff has failed to' prove any such gift made in its favour. Rather, the CS Khatian No. 473/1 (exhibit-uma) adduced by the defendant clearly proves that 16 annas of the suit land originally belonged to ভারত সম্রাট পক্ষে পাবলিক ওয়ার্কস ডিপার্টমেন্ট i.e. the government, not by Hindu Zaminders. This evidence on record repudiates the case that any Hindu Zaminder was owner of the suit property or that they could have made any gift in respect of the said property without a registered deed of gift and that both the Courts below have utterly failed to read this evidence and to appreciate that the CS Khatian No. 473/1 (exhibit-uma) proves that original title of the suit land lies in the government represented by the Department of Public Works, which is now under the Ministry of Public Works & Housing Settlement of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 16. The appellate Court has also failed to appreciate that the onus to prove its title and right in the suit properties entirely lies upon the plaintiff and this position of law has also been re-iterated in the case of Noor Mohammad Khan vs Government of Bangladesh, reported in 42 DLR 434. 

 17. Besides, it is also settled law that the' Court cannot, in passing a judgment and decree, invent or rely upon a third case, as has been done in this case by introducing a case of adverse possession. The Courts below have also failed to appreciate that, adverse possession, in a case, can at best be pleaded in defence, but the plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree of declaration of a title based on adverse pos- session. In the case between Shaikh Lota & Kamal Baksh vs Siraj Bakshi, reported in 7 BLT (AD) 328, it has been held that, adverse possession does not entitle the plaintiff to get a decree of declaration of title on adverse possession, whereas the trial Court has passed the impugned judgment and decree holding that the plaintiff has acquired title and ownership in the suit land at least based on adverse possession and the appellate Court, in its impugned judgment and decree, has utterly failed to appreciate the law declared in 7 BLT (AD) 328, though cited before it, and affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The appellate Court has not taken into consideration its obligation to abide by the law declared by the Appellate Division, which is binding on the Courts below as per Article 111 of the Constitution. It is pertinent to record here that in the case reported in 8 LG (2011) (AD) page 70, Bangladesh vs Helal Jute Press Ltd; it has been held that, the decision of the Appellate Division is binding upon all Courts of Bangladesh and no Court can ignore it. If he does so, it may not only be contemptuous but also tantamounts to violation of the constitution. 

 18. Then taking for consideration the positive case of the plaintiff that they have acquired title and ownership in the suit land on the basis of gift made in their favour by the then Hindu Zaminders, both the Courts below have found that no such gift has been proved by the plaintiff by adducing any evidence. The appellate Court as well as the trial Court ought to have recorded that in order to create or to extinguish any right or title in any landed property a registered deed, as per provision of section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908 was a must and they ought not to have found any title and ownership of the plaintiff based on adverse possession, which was not the case of plaintiff. 

 20. As such, we are of the view that, in passing the impugned judgments and decrees, instead of declaring any right, title or ownership in the suit land the Courts below have conferred in the plaintiff right, title and ownership in the suit properties, which is not within the ambit of section 42 of the SR Act, 1877. 

 21. Looking at the documentary evidence, Exhibit-Umma and Umma-1 which are the CS Khatian No. 471/1 and the corresponding SA Khatian No.7 of Mouja Helatola, Police Station and District-Khulna, comprising CS Plot No. 45/117, corresponding to SA Plot No. 169, we find that these evidences clearly prove that 0.28 acres of land in the CS Khatian has been recorded in the name of the Government of India (ভারত সম্রাট) represented by its Public Works Department as the owner and name of the President Coronation Hall Committee has been recorded as the occupant of the sixteen annas of the suit land. In the corresponding SA Khatian No.7 name of President Coronation Hall Committee has been recorded for sixteen annas of the suit land, although in the CS Khatian the Coronation Hall Committee was a mere occupant or licensee as distinguished from a tenure-holder or Raiyat only to use the suit property for the specific purpose to observe the event of coronation by a committee formed to that end, namely-Coronation Hall Committee, Khulna. This factual position is also supported and corroborated by the SA Khatian No. 7 submitted and proved by the plaintiff itself and marked as Exhibit-2. The possession of Coronation Hall Committee in the suit land is further supported by Exhibit-4 series, which are the land development tax receipts from Bangla 1386 to 1408 and all in the name of defendant, submitted and proved by the plaintiff. All these rent receipts (খাজনা দাখিলা) are in the name of Coronation Hall Committee, Khulna. Besides, the City Corporation tax receipts in the name of the defendant, (exhibit 6 series) adduced and proved by the plaintiff, also support the defence case. As such the positive case of the defendant that the suit land as well as the properties thereon has been recorded in CS Khatian and in the RS Khatian are in the name of the defendant and that Khazana (land development tax) and the holding tax in respect of the suit properties are being paid by the defendant have been proved before the trial Court. But both the Courts below have found the plaintiff in possession, which is contrary to the documentary evidence on record and this clearly makes out the case of non-reading and misreading of evidence on record by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court, as the last Court of fact. Hence, the findings, as to the title and possession, arrived at by the Courts below, are contrary to the evidence on record and are perverse, hence liable to be reversed. 

 22. In this regard we find no reason to depart from the view taken in Noor Mohammad vs The State, reported in 42 DLR 434, wherein it has been held that plaintiffs having failed to prove their possession in the suit land, a simple suit for declaration of their title is barred. But the appellate Court, although referred to this decision in its judgment, has simply brushed aside the law declared by this Court, which it ought to have followed in this particular case. But, for its failure in appreciating the law and the evidence on record, it has committed error of law in affirming the impugned judgment and decrees that has resulted in error in the impugned judgment and decree occasioning failure of justice. 

 23. The Court below as well as the appellate Court, as the last Court of facts, have also failed to appreciate and to interpret Exhibit-9 and 9(Ka) showing that the defendant Coronation Hall Committee, as the land lord and the LESSOR, has executed agreements, dated 06-3-1952 and 15-3-1971 respectively; letting out the Coronation Hall, except the green room attached to the stage, from time to time to its tenant. Agreement dated 06-3-1952 (exhibit- 9) records that it was a renewal of an earlier lease to the same lessee by the lessor Coronation Hall Committee. These documentary evidence also clearly proves the title and the uninterrupted and possession of the defendant in the suit properties, but both the trial Court and the appellate Court have failed to interpret these documentary evidence and had passed the impugned judgments, and decrees in favour of the plaintiff, based on findings which are contrary to the evidence on record, hence perverse and liable to be interfered with and be set-aside. Moreover, such findings are also repugnant to the law declared in 4 BLT (AD) 150, discussed below. 

 24. We have also taken for consideration the receipts/bills paid to the Power Development Board of Bangladesh, which have been marked as Exhibit- 12 series. These exhibits show that the plaintiff organization has paid electric bills, monthly consumption of which ranges in between Tk. 180 to Tk. 556. These receipts, showing payment of bills for consuming electricity are not document, either to prove title or possession as incidence of title to the suit property. It, at best, shows that the consumer of the electricity in certain premises has paid bills to Power Development Board for consumption of the electricity, either as tenant or hirer or as licensee, as the case may be. It does not help much the plaintiff's case who has failed to prove any basis of their title or possession as incidence of its title in the suit properties. 

 25. To controvert the contention of the plaintiff, the appellant-petitioner has submitted 51 DLR 435 (Abdul Kader vs Abdullah) wherein it has been held that, in a suit for declaration of title, mere possession of the property is not sufficient, unless the plaintiff can produce a document of title showing his acquisition of right, title and interest in the suit property. We find no reason to take a view different from this view, though taken by a single Bench, inasmuch as the law laid down in this decision is sound and accepted position of law as would be noticed from the decision reported in 4 BLT (AD) (1996) 150 (Md. Banzir Ahmed vs Debendra Chandra Saha.) 

 27. We have also noticed that, when the CS and SA Khatians and the khajanadhakila adduced and proved before the trial Court clearly prove the possession arid prima facie title of the defendant, the plaintiff has filed this suit for declaration simpliciter, without asking for consequential relief and without payment of advalorume Court fees, upon proper valuation of the suit. But the trial Court as well as the appellate Court have failed to appreciate this defect in the suit and have failed to find that the suit, as filed and valued, was not maintainable in its present form and was liable to be dismissed under the proviso to section 42 of the Special Relief Act, 1877 as well as for want of proper valuation and nonpayment of advalorume Court fees. 

 28. In 42 DLR 434 it has been held that the plaintiff having failed to prove their possession in the suit land, a simple suit for declaration of title is barred. This decision was also cited by the defendant-petitioner, because it supports the defence case. In another case 4 BLT (AD) 150 (Md. Banzer Ahmed vs Debendra Chandra Saha), it has been held that "In a suit for declaration of title mere possession of the property is not sufficient unless the plaintiff can produce a document of title showing his acquisition of right, title and interest in the suit property." Similar views was taken by a single bench as has been referred to by the petitioner and quoted herein above. This law thus declared by the Appellate Division reported in 4 BLT (AD) f 50; rather supports case of the petitioner and goes against the plaintiff. 

 30. Looking into the decisions cited by the plaintiff-opposite parties we find that 18 DLR 691 and 54 DLR 354 are not applicable to this case. The first cited case is a case where the plaintiff was disposed by the defendant who had no title to the suit property and the second case is a case of claiming title and possession based on allotment letter issued in favour of the plaintiff. There is no similarity between the facts and circumstances of those cases and the case before us. 

 31. We have also considered other cases cited by the opposite parties. In 35 DLR (AD) 216, it has been held that "Rent receipts are evidence of possession, and may be used as collateral evidence of title." In the case before us the rent receipts which are Exhibit-4 series, are in the name of the defendant and accordingly these are collateral evidence of title of the defendant, not of the plaintiff. So, it does not help the plaintiff. In 42 DLR (AD) 225, it has been held that the defendants have no burden to prove their alternative story. We do not find how this decision supports the plaintiff's case, instead of helping the defendant-petitioner. 

 32. In view of our deliberation and findings recorded herein above, we find that the findings of fact arrived at by the trial Court and as affirmed by the appellate Court are wholly contrary to the evidence on record, based on misreading and non-reading of evidence and the same are perverse, hence liable to be interfered with and be reversed, in exercise of revisional jurisdiction of this Court. We are also of the view that, in passing the impugned judgment and decree the appellate Court has committed error of law, resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The appellate Court, itself ought to have assessed the evidence and reversed the findings of the Court below, set-aside the judgment and decree dated 08-6-2005, passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna and should have dismissed the Title Suit No. 49 of 2002. 

 In the result, this rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. Judgment and decrees of both the Courts below are hereby set-aside and the Title Suit No. 49 of 2002 of the Court of Joint District Judge, Khulna is hereby dismissed. The Deputy Commissioner, Khulna is directed, in exercise of the power vested in this Court under section 151 and 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Article 101 and 109 of the Constitution, to get corrected the SA and the subsequent Khatians in connection with suit property and to record the suit property, in Khash Khatian, in the name of the government represented by the Ministry of Public Works. Concerned Assistant Commissioner Land and the Tahshil Office, Kanungo are directed to record the suit property in Khas Khatian, towards performance of their duty as per Article 112 of the Constitution. The suit property should be managed by the Coronation Hall Committee, Khulna in the manner as before, as a management body on behalf of the government, until otherwise decided by the government. Let, copies of this judgment be sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Law to issue a circular in the light of the law declared by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 8 LG (2011) (AD) 70 for information and compliance of the learned Judges of the sub-ordinate Courts. Let copies of the judgment also be sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works, Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh and to the Deputy Commissioner, Khulna for necessary steps for recording the suit property in Khash Khatian.

parties:
Abdus Samad Khan ------ Appellant
vs
Dulal Chandra Ghose and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The appellant instituted Title Suit No. 153 of 1982 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) 1st Court, Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The above Court having found that the summons of the above suit were duly served upon both the Government and the respondent No. 1 on 19-5-1982 and 17-7-1982 respectively, posted the above suit for hearing but the hearing of the suit was adjourned on 19-8-1982, 21-9-1982 and 22-11-1982 and it was ultimately taken up for hearing on 23-1-1983 and decreed ex parte on 15-2-1983. Then on depositing the balance consideration money on 6-9-1983 the appellant filed Execution Case No.30 of 1983. Subsequently the above execution case, being transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Gazipur, was re-numbered as Execution Case No. 13 of 1985 and then sale deed was executed and registered on 13-5-1985 through Court. The respondent No. 1 then filed miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1988 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, (now Joint District Judge), 1st Court, Dhaka on 9-1-1988 for restoration of the above Title Suit No. 153 of 1982 to its original file and number on setting aside the ex parte decree dated 15-2-1983 on the ground that he never entered into any contract with the appellant for sale of the suit land and he had no knowledge of the suit and that he filed the miscellaneous case within time from the date of his knowledge. The said case, on transfer to Gazipur, was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 14 of 1988. The appellant filed written objection in the above case totally denying the statements made by the respondent No. 1 in the above miscellaneous case. The learned Subordinate Judge by judgment and order dated 30-5-1991 dismissed the miscellaneous case holding that the same is barred by limitation. Then the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment, allowed the appeal upon setting aside the judgment of the trial Court and restored Title Suit No. 153 of 1982 to its file and number. 

 3. Leave was granted on the submission that the trial Court found that although it is difficult to determine whether the original defendant received the summons of the original suit or not but it has been established by evidence on record that the defendant-respondent received summons of Title Execution Case No. 30 of 1983 on 12-12-83 and, as such, he had knowledge of the original suit on 12-12-1983 but he filed the instant miscellaneous case on 9-1-1988 i.e. five years after his knowledge of the original suit and the submission that the High Court Division did not reverse the finding of the trial Court to the effect that the original defendant received the summons of Title Execution Case No. 30 of 1983 on 12-12-1983 and the High Court Division also erroneously ignoring this factum of knowledge of the original defendant, and relying solely upon the service of summons of the original suit and on other irrelevant considerations, allowed the appeal without meeting the finding of the trial Court to the effect that the miscellaneous case is barred by limitation on the ground of not filing the case within 30 days from the date of the knowledge of the original defendants on 12-12-1983. 

 5. As it appears admittedly the summons of Title Execution Case No. 30 of 1983 were served upon the respondent No. 1 on 12-12-1983 and the same amply proves the date of knowledge of the respondent No. 1 of the original Title Suit No. 153 of 1982 on 12-12-1983 but he filed the instant Miscellaneous Case No. 5 of 1988 on 9-1-88 i.e. long 5 years after the date of his knowledge of the original suit and the High Court Division erroneously ignored this factum of knowledge of the respondent No. 1 of the original suit and relying on the absence of proof of service of summons of the original suit upon the appellant and other irrelevant considerations allowed the appeal. It also appears that the High Court Division did not meet the reasoning’s of the trial Court and also did not consider that the miscellaneous case is barred by limitation on the ground of not filing the miscellaneous case within 30 days from date of the knowledge of original defendant i.e. on 12-12-1983. It further appears that the appellant though sufficiently established about the service of summons of the execution case upon the respondent No. 1, the High Court Division, without considering the provision of Article 164 of the Limitation Act, allowed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 613 of 1991 setting aside the ex-parte decree. So the judgment and order of the High Court Division cannot be sustained.

parties:
Mrs. Shahida Begum, Wife of Ibrahim Mia
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and other
full_judgment:
2. It is stated in the writ petition that one Syed' Abdul Waheed acquired ownership in the aforesaid holding No. 10.3, Block-B, Iqubal Road, Dhaka by virtue of 99 years lease vide lease deed No. 16348 dated 30.12.1963 by the Government of the then East Pakistan. While said Syed Abdul Waheed had been residing with his family in the house on the said holding he executed a registered deed of Power of Attorney dated 21.8.72 in favour of Paster David Paul Rema, Secretary of Bangladesh Section of Seventh Day Adventists, a Christan Missionary organization situated at Mirpur, Dhaka authorizing him to look after and sell the said house property as he had to go abroad and he had no other relation in Bangladesh to look after and sell the same. Said Paster David Paul Rema as the constituted Attorney of Syed Abdul Waheed while in occupation and possession of the said house sold the same to Lawrence Bennett under five registered sale deed. Nos. 2880 dated 29.6.1979, 2884 dated 30.6.1979, 2895 dated 2.7.1999, 2896 dated 2.7.1979 and 3209 dated 20.7.1979. Meanwhile, possession of the said house was forcibly taken over from Pasteur David Paul in 1975 by some miscreants with the help of corrupt government officials and the government then enlisted the said house as an abandoned property towards the end of 1975. Accordingly, said Paster David Paul Rema and Lowrance Benett in Iurn submitted applications with the Ministry of Works for release of the said house without any success. Thereafter said Lowrance Benett being in need of money sold the said house property to the petitioner, Mrs. Shahida Begum by a registered sale deed No. 1980 dated 20.9.87 and handed over all the basic documents of title to him in original. After the purchase the petitioner came to know that the said house was already included in the "Ka" list as an abandoned building vide serial No. 21, Page 9762(15) of the gazette dated 23.9.1986. The petitioner then filed an application under section 7 of the said Ordinance 1985 for release of the said house by excluding the same from the "Ka' list of the said gazette. But the Court of Settlement refused to entertain the application on the ground of limitation. Against this backdrop, the petitioner filed the writ petition and obtained the present Rule. 

 4. We have perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavit together with the annexures. The petitioner has filed the certified copy of the Lease deed dated 13.12.63, certified copy of the registered Power of Attorney, five original sale deed dated 29.6.79, 30.6.79, 2.7.79 and 20.7.79 showing sale of the said house by Mr. Paster david Paul Rema to Lowrance Benett and a certified copy of the sale deed dated 29.6.87 showing sale of the said house by Lowrance Bennett to the petitioner. It appears from the record vide Annexure-I to the Supplementary Affidavit sworn on 11.1.2005 by the petitioner that the petitioner filed all the basic documents of title to the said house property with the Ministry of Housing and Public Works pursuant to the Ministry's letter dated 14.8.2000 vide Annexure-"H" to the writ petition. It is therefore claimed and submitted on behalf of the petitioner that she could not file the lease deed and the power of attorney in original before this Court. 

 5. We find from the record that the respondent No. 1, Ministry of Works, by Memo. No. 10-1, S-1-2000-1868 dated 14.8.2000 asked the petitioner to submit her original documents in support of her claim to the house in question and pursuant thereto the petitioner by a letter dated 25.8.2000, Annexure-"I" to the supplementary affidavit, addressed to Nasreen Akhter, Senior Assistant Secretary, Ministry of Works, Wing 10 sub-mitted all her documents of title in original. It is argued that the original owner of the said house authorized his Constituted Attorney, Paster Davit Paul Rema, to look after and sell the said house by a registered power of attorney dated 21.8.1972. Original of this power of attorney appears to have been submitted with the Ministry of Works as indicated above. By virtue of this power of attorney the said Constituted attorney sold the said house to one Lawrence Benett by five registered sale deeds in 1979 as mentioned above. It also appears that the said original sale deeds have also been submitted by the petitioner to the ministry of works. Subsequently, the petitioner bought the said house from Lowrance benett by a registered sale deed No. 1980 dated 29.6.87. 

 6. It is asserted by the petitioner that the Constituted Attorney, Paster David Paul Rema, while continuing in possession of the said house, was dispossessed by some miscreants in 1975. Accordingly, said David Paul Rema by a letter dated 9.5.75 and thereafter Lawrence Bennet by another letter dated 20.6.81 made representation for release of the said house from the list of the abandoned property but without any success. Since all the original papers including the lease deed dated 30.12.63 and the original registered Power of Attorney No. 14940 dated 21.8.72 are in possession of the petitioner it is highly probable that the original owner of the said house Syed Abdul Waheed was present and available in Bangladesh till after 28.2.72 i.e. when he executed and registered the said Power of Attorney in favour of the Paster David Paul Rema authorizing him to sell the same while he was going abroad. The legal position is that the original owner of the said house Abdul Waheed was in Bangladesh even after 28.2.72 and accordingly the said house was not and still could not be considered and treated as an abandoned property under P.O. 16 of 1972. 

 7. No materials have been brought on record by the respondent government to dislodge the aforesaid legal and factual aspect of the case and further the respondent 'government did not form any opinion whether the original owner of the said house, Syed Abdul Waheed, left Bangladesh and was absent from before 28.2.72 and his staying abroad from Bangladesh after 28.2.72 was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. Furthermore, we also do not find any thing on record that the respondent government took over possession of the said house as an abandoned property for the reason that it was left uncured for by its owner nor any notice as required under Article 7 of P.O. 16 of 1972 was issued on any occupant of the house before the possession of the said house was taken over as an abandoned property. In that view of the matter, subsequent inclusion of the said house in the 'Ka' list as an abandoned property under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 without issuing of any notice as contemplated under section 4 of the said Ordinance is illegal and without jurisdiction. Hence the inclusion of the house in question in "Ka" list is illegal. Because it is held in the case of Lutfunnessa Vs. Bangladesh 42 DLR(AD)86 that to justify inclusion of any building in the lists of abandoned buildings published in the official Gazette the government must show that the possession of the building was taken over at same point of time as an abandoned property. It is also held in the case of Helaluddin Ahmed 4 MLR (AD) 140 that when no notice was served and pursuant thereto no possession of the building was taken over by the government, the enlistment is invalid and in that case the petitioner was not required to go to the Court of Settlement. In view of the aforesaid legal position, the enlistment of the house in question is without lawful authority. 

 9. It has been held by the Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh V. Amela Khatoon reported in 53 DLR(AD)55 that in case where the petitioner is found in possession of the basic documents of title in original it becomes highly probable that the original owner was in Bangladesh even after 28.2.72 and while in Bangladesh she caused the said house to be sold to Lowrance Banett and thereafter to the petitioner. As against this the respondent government has not been able to make out any case on fact and law that the said house is an abandoned property liable to be included in the "Ka" list as per law. Hence, we have no hesitation to hold that this house is not an abandoned house and as such it was not liable to be included in the "Ka" list. The

caseno: Civil petition for leave to appeal no. 3135 OF 2014
parties:
Terab Ali and others -------- Petitioners
VERSUS
Syed Ullah and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Nuruzzaman, J: 1. This Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 19.05.2014 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3437 of 2012 discharging the Rule and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 15.07.2012 passed by the learned Special District Judge, Sylhet in Civil Revision No.3 of 2012, rejecting the revisional application and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 11.01.2012 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet in Title Execution Case No.3 of 1993, rejecting the petition filed by the petitioner-judgment debtors praying for dismissal of the execution case as being time barred. 

 2. The facts, leading to filing this Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal, in short, are that the respondent Nos.1-8 herein as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.22 of 1983 impleading the defendants for declaration of their title in the suit land, as well as for recovery of khas possession. The principal defendants (petitioners of this petition) submitted written statement in that suit but ultimately did not contest. Accordingly, the said suit was decreed ex-parte on 15.04.1989. For setting aside the said ex-parte decree dated 15.04.1989, the judgment debtors instituted Miscellaneous Case No.36 of 1989 under order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 15.05.1989 which was dismissed for default on 23.05.1989. Thereafter, for setting aside the said ex-parte decree, the judgment debtors as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.53 of 1995, in the same Court praying for a decree declaring that the said ex-parte judgment passed in the said Title Suite No.22 of 1989 is not binding upon them for the reason that the decree passed in that suit was obtained by practicing fraud upon the Court. The said suit was dismissed and against the judgment of dismissal of that suit, they preferred Title Appeal No.309 of 2012 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet, and the said appeal was also dismissed. Against such judgment of dismissal of the said appeal, they preferred Civil Revision No.6615 of 2002, before the High Court Division and obtained a Rule. At the time of issuance of the Rule, the High Court Division stayed further proceeding of aforesaid Title Execution Case No.03 of 1983. Ultimately, the Rule issued in the said Civil Revision No.6615 of 2002 was discharged by judgment and order dated 17.12.2009 and the order of stay was vacated. The further case is that the respondent Nos.1-8 herein as plaintiffs decree holders, instituted the Title Execution Case No.3 of 1993 in the original Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet on 21.10.1993 praying for execution of the ex-parte decree obtained by them on 15-04-1989 in Title Suit No.22 of 1989 against the petitioners and the opposite Party Nos.9-52 as judgment debtors stating that as there is no legal impediments against the execution of the original judgment and decree the Decree Holders have filed this Title Execution Case. 

 3. The Judgment Debtors have filed a petition supported with verification on 27.02.2011 for disallowing the execution case. They have averred on that petition that the present Title Execution Case has been filed on the basis of ex-parte decree of Title Suit no. 22 of 1983 passed on 15.04.1989. But the decree holders have filed the instant Title Execution Case on expiry of the specified there years. Thus the instant execution case is barred by limitation and liable to be disallowed. 

 4. The Decree Holders have filed a written objection against the said petition of the Judgment Debtor. The Decree Holders have averred in their written objection that the original Title Suit no. 22 of 1983 has been decreed on declaring title and recovery of possession against the Judgment Debtors. The Defendants-Judgment Debtors filed written statement on the original suit but did not contest. That's why that suit has been decreed ex parte. The Defendants-Judgment Debtors filed Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and that was disallowed on 23.11.1993. Thereafter the Decree Holders have filed this Execution Case on 8.11.1993. The Judgment Debtor as Plaintiffs filed Title Suit 53 of 1995 to declare the ex parte judgment decree of T.S. 22.83 as void, collusive, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff of Title Suit 52 of 1995. That suit no. 53 of 95 has been dismissed on contest on 12.8.1999. Thereafter, the judgment debtors-defendant filed Title Appeal no. 309 of 1999 and that appeal has also been disallowed. The judgment debtors/defendants filed Civil Revision no. 6615 of 02 and the proceedings of this execution case has been stayed till disposal of the Civil Revision. And then High Court Division disallowed that civil revision with as follows- 

 "And it is further ordered that the order of stay passed by this court staying all further proceedings of Title Execution case No. 3 of 1993 now pending in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sylhet is hereby vacated". As such, they prayed for disallowance of the petition. 

 10. Mr. Chanchal Kummar Biswas, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the High Court Division failed to consider that the miscellaneous case is not a continuation of the suit and the very first execution case was barred by limitation and the unreported decision of a case as passed in Civil Revision No.4949 of 2001 and the decision referred by the High Court Division are not at all applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. He further submits that the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 22 of 1983 on 15.04.1989 and the execution case has been filed on 20.10.1993 which is beyond the period of 3 years as codified by the article 182 of limitation Act, 1908. The learned Executing Court relied on a synopsis of a decision of High Court Division of Pakistan passed in 1998, published in a D.L.R. reference book, though the decision has neither binding effect nor is applicable in the instant case after independence. And reliance on reference book is not legal. Moreover, the decision appears as stare decisis in the Pakistan contest and learned special District Judge as well as the High Court Division failed to consider it. He next submits that the learned Courts below failed to consider that there has been a great change in Limitation Act in Pakistan after 1971. In Pakistan the Article 182 of the Limitation Act has been omitted and there is no other provision for limitation regarding filing of execution proceeding except article 181 and according to the provision of article 181 of Limitation Act of Pakistan, limitation starts, when the right to apply accrues, and learned Executing Court failed to realise that the decision relied on has been passed under Article 181 of the Limitation Act of Pakistan. But in our Limitation Act, there is specific provision for limitation for filing execution proceedings prescribing 3 years from the date of the decree or order and where there has been appeal from the date of final decree or order of appellate court or withdrawal of appeal or where there has been a review of the judgment from the date of the decision passed in review or where the decree has been amended the date of amendment etc. No where the period of miscellaneous case under order 9 rule 13 or any other miscellaneous case under order 41 rules 19 and 21 has been included. From the decision referred by the judgment debtors in ILR VOL LIV page 1052, it is found that though the period of limitation of appeal is included but the period of miscellaneous appeal has been omitted. Both the courts below fails realize it. He last submits that all the statements made in the written objection filed the decree holders against the petition dated 27.02.2011 filed by the judgment-debtors, is not correct. The miscellaneous case under order 9 rule 13 has been dismissed for failure of taking steps of service of notices and subsequent Title suit no. 53 of 1995 challenging the ex-parte decree on the ground of fraud etc. has failed due to the latches of the engaged lawyer and the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 22 of 1989 is nonexecutable and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. 

 13. As per Article 182 of the Limitation Act, 1908 the very first execution case must be filed within 03 (three) years of the date of decree. And admittedly as well as documentarily the Title Execution case in question bearing no. 03 of 1993 was filed on 20.10.1993 where as the original Title Suit no. 22 of 1989 was decree ex-parte on 15.04.1989 which makes the Title Execution case no. 03 of 1993 hopelessly barred by limitations for at least 01 and half years. We surprising observed that all the courts below missed the clear and unambiguous provisions of law.
