full_judgment:
Respondents filed Title Suit No. 163 of 1968 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, against the defendants praying for partition of the suit lands on declaration of the plaintiffs title in certain share of the suit lands. 

 3. Plaintiffs case is that after the death of Hedayet his daughter and widow left the property to the care of Jobeda who possessed the property for and on behalf of the co-sharer and the plaintiffs are thus in constructive possession of the suit land. The ejmali character or the suit land has been causing inconvenience, hence the suit for partition with a prayer for declaration of the plaintiffs title. 

 4. Defendants 1 to 7 contested the suit by filing a written statement. They claimed through late Alfazuddin Ahmed who purchased the property from Jobeda Khatun in 1939, Their case was that Jobeda alone possessed the entire suit land exclusively and adversely in open assertion over the title thereto. Hedayet never possessed the suit land. Jobeda Khatun earlier mortgaged by way of conditional sale 7 pakhis of laud in 1935 and subsequently sold the said laud to Alfazuddin Ahmed in 1939. Thus Alfazuddin acquired  by purchase the entire suit land. Till his death in 1962 he executed as many as 7 registered kabuliyats during the period of 1936-1961 and after his death his heirs defendants 1 to 7 had been possessing the land on payment of rent exclusively for more than 12 year; in assertion of their hostile title to the knowledge of all including the heirs of Hedayet Baksha. 

 6. The appellate court below, however. decreed the suit after setting aside the Judgment and decree of the trial court and decreed the suit of the plaintiffs for partition, on declaration of the title to the extent of 5 pakhis 2 gondas 2 karas and 2 krants out of the lands shown in the schedule. 

 7. It is admitted that Elahi Baksha, husband of Jobeda Khatun, had two brothers, Hedayet Baksha and Rebat Baksha and one sister Jarina. Elahi Baksha died leaving his widow Jobeda and children. Hedayet died in 1934 or 1935 leaving his wife and 2 daughters, who are the plaintiffs. Rehat Baksha survived by his heirs who are defendants 8 to 14 and Jarina left behind her heirs defendants 15 to 19. Defendants 22 to 41 have been impleaded since they are the owners of the rest of the land and they have been made parties as the suit was one for partition. Elahi Baksha lived at the residence of his father-in-law at Kaliganj where he died in 1320 B.S. leaving his wife Jobeda Khatun and children. It seems after the death of Elahi Baksha his brother Hedayet Baksha lived in the house of Jobeda's father for some time and looked after her affairs. The land in C. S. Khatian No. 105 (5.16 acres of land) of mouza Kaliganj originally belonged to one Yunus Bepari, who settled with Jobeda Khatun, wife of late Elahi Baksha 13½ pakhis of lands equivalent to 3.1 acres and with Hedayet Baksha 6½ pakhis of land equivalent to 1.69 acres by accepting from them a joint registered kabuliyat dated 9th jaistha 1327 B.S. corresponding to 2.6.1920. Since that settlement both the tenants possessed In ejmali the entire 20 pakis of land which is the suit land . 

 9. Alfazuddin Ahmed died on 12.11.62 The suit was filed in 1968. As noticed that the heirs of Hedayet Baksha are now the plaintiffs and the heirs of Alfazuddin Ahmed are the defendants. The trial court came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs had failed to prove their case and the suit was hopelessly time barred, and as such the plaintiffs are not entitled to get any decree. Further Hedayat and his heirs were never recognised as tenants by the landlords and as such Hedayet Baksha or his heirs never acquired any interest in the suit property. 

 10. The appellate court, on the other band, came to the conclusion that the right, title and interest by Hedayet Baksha in 6½  pakhis of land out of tile suit land had been subsisting and they had not been extinguished in any manner and consequently the plaintiffs inherited their legal share from Hedayet and they are entitled to get the same. The appellate court below further found that the defence has totally failed to prove that they ever set up a hostile title against the plaintiffs or their predecessor to their knowledge more than 12 years before the institution of this suit. Evidence of P.Ws. 1,3 and 4 was considered, which showed that the plaintiff’s had knowledge of the sale of the suit land by Jobeda Khatun although there was no evidence when the plaintiffs derived the knowledge of the same. Knowledge of Rehat Baksha, who was the husband of the sister of Alfazuddin as attesting witness of Exts. E. and E(1) could not be the knowledge of the plaintiff. Considering this relationship the appellate court below observed "there is no doubt that he was very much well affected to Alfazuddin Ahmed," Alfazuddin Ahmed immediately after his purchase created temporary lease by as many as 7 kabuliyats exts. B series through different persons in respect of the suit laud from 1936 to 1961. The appellate court below commented that by successive transfer by Exts. B series he thought, wrongly though "that he would thereby be in a position to extinguish, the title of Hedayet and his heirs." The appellate court below carefully considered the evidence and came to the conclusion that the right, title and interest of Hedayet Baksha had subsisted and his heirs are entitled to demand partition. Accordingly, the suit was decreed. 

 The High Court Division repelled the contention of adverse possession and considered the possession of a co-owner becomes adverse to other co-owners from the moment when there is an outer or exclusion, that is, an assertion of a hostile title by one co-owner as against the others and that to the knowledge of the latter. It was noticed that these elements bad not been proved by the defendants. Sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession, Reliance was placed on long line of decisions specially in the case of Bindu Bala De Vs. Rebati Mohan De reported in 4 DLR 293. In this view of the matter. the order and judgment of the appellate court below was affirmed and the suit was decreed. 

 12. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellants argued since 1939 Alfazuddin is in possession after his purchase Vide Exts. F and F (1) and therefore, his possession will be adverse to the plaintiffs. Mr. Pal argued that the defendants were in possession openly and to the knowledge of the plaintiff and such overt act is enough to constitute as ouster. Reliance was placed on some highest authorities claiming title by adverse possession 46 I.A. 46 and 61 LA. 78. Mr. Pal further argued that conception or Hindu caste cannot be imported in the facts of this case nor of law of agency can be applied, inasmuch as, no relevant evidence was given on that point. The question of equity does not come, it is contended, since it is the law that should be applied. Mr. Pal argued heavily on two decisions 23 Bom 137 and AIR 1942 Mad (F.B.) 622. 

 14. Now the second phase: on 10.8.38 Qayum sold his mortgaged land to Alfazuddin and on 12.4.39 Jobeda Khatun sold her mortgaged land to Alfazuddin. Now third phase: from 1939 to 1962 it seems that the parties were not at loggerheads. It was only in 1968 that the suit was filed. Mr. Ahmed argued that there is no trouble so far as the defendants are concerned because it is the matter between the relations and the suit land is situated at a distance of one mile of the plaintiffs' residence. Evidence was given that the plaintiffs got usufruct from the defendents, Finding of fact of the appellate court below and the High Court Division are that Hedayet had a title. Till Hedayet's death no case of adverse possession was made out and after Alfazuddin's purchase he became a co-sharer. Therefore, the question of adverse possession does not arise. Mr. Ahmed contended that the criticism tint plaintiffs obtained usufruct from time to time is not based on the pleading does not merit consideration, in as much as, positive evidence had been given by the plaintiffs that they not only had cordial relationship with Jobeda Khatun and Atfazuddin, but they were given also the usufruct from time to time. Evidence is there even in 1965 that usufruct was demanded from Jobeda. In this view of the evidence it is contended that the defendants had failed to make out achy case of adverse possession. 

 15. The plaintiff’s case was that the suit lands are ejmali and a co-sharer’s possession of ejmali property is the possession of all co-sharers. Since it has become inconvenient to possess the land in ejmali they brought the suit for partition. The defendants case was that Jobeda had been possessing the entire 20 pakhis of land in her exclusive raiyati rights on payment of rent in her name for the entire and on open assertion of hostile right and title against others. Hedayet, brother of Elahi Baksha staking advantage of illiteracy of the pardanashyn Jobeda Khatun fraudulently managed to create the kabuliyat in question and put forth a claim over the suit property in an attempt to make illegal gains" and Alfazuddin purchased the entire 20 pakhis for good consideration and since his purchase possessed the same "openly and publicly adversely to all subject to the right of Jobeda Knatun and Abdul Qayum for repurchase." In the additional written statement a further stand was taken that though Jobeda drove out Hedayet on detection of the fraud "who appeared to have fraudulently joined in a kabuliyat taking advantage of his position and no heir of Hedayet ever possessed any part of the suit land aid they had no right title or interest in the suit property. 

 18. The High Court Division rightly took the view that possession of a co-owner became adverse to others co-owners from the moment from when there is an ouster or exclusion. Reliance was placed in the case of Maharaja Bhupendra Ch. Singha Sarma & ors. Vs. Sudhindra Ch. Singha & ors reported in 5 D.L.R. 251. The appellate court below also worded a finding that there was nothing to suggest ouster or exclusion of the plaintiffs from possession. Sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession. The appellate court below took the view that Hedayet possessed the suit land jointly with Jobeda. These findings of the courts below are founded on the evidence and taking into consideration of the facts and circumstances the question emerged whether the possession of the defendants were so hostile and adverse openly so as to justify the claim of adverse possession. Even if there are apparent show of adverse possession whether those circumstances were sufficient to defeat the title of the real owner only because some lack of vigilance can be attributed to the plaintiffs and would in such circumstances relieve the defendant from discharging their onus in support of their claim of adverse possession The onus is very heavy. It is for the defendant to discharge this so as to build up a claim of adverse possession. A thin veneer of adverse possession or semblance of it viewed from the distance would not be sufficient for the defendants to succeed without discharging their heavy onus. They have to do more that their possession was so open and hostile to the knowledge of all that the plaintiffs must have known the notorious fact that the plea of adverse possession is being raised up. When the relationships are such that the co-sharers are led to believe in certain circumstances which are not uncommon as fact of We will those circumstances be taken as evidence of knowledge of adverse possession. Long line of decisions show that is not the case. Plaintiffs' evidence that they got share of their crop from Alfazuddin and prior to that from Jobeda cannot be disbelieved when viewed in the light of relationship. Mere non-payment of rents and even non-sharing of profit would got justify a case of adverse possession. 

 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.--I have gene through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother, B.H. Chowdhury-J, but I regret my inability to agree with him. I would therefore give my own judgment as follows: This is defendants' appeal. The principal question therein is whether the High Court Division is well founded in law and fact in rejecting their contention that the plaintiff's suit for title and partition is barred by limitation under Article 144 of the Limitation Act in view of their alleged adverse possession of over 30 years as Stranger-Purchaser of the whole of the joint property. 

 23. The suit land measuring 20 pakhis, equivalent to 5.21 acres, originally belonged to one Younus Bepari. Plaintiffs' (respondents) case is that this laud was settled in raiyati right to Jobeda Khatun and Hedayet Baksh under a registered kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920; share of Jobeda Khatun was 14½  pakhis and that of Hedayet Baksh was 6½  pakhis. Both Jobeda and Hedayet Baksh possessed the land jointly. Hedayet, who lived in Jobeda's house in village Kaliganj left this village and settled in village Zinjira a few miles away but he continued to possess the land jointly with Jobeda till he died sometime in 1933-1934 AD. On his death his widow and two daughters (who are the plaintiffs)along with his brother Rabat Baksh and sister Jarina inherited his 6½  pakhis and since then they had been in constructive possession of the land through Jabeda.  Jabeda transferred five pakhis of land front her share to her son Abdul Qaayum by a registered Deed of Gift dated 5 September 1934. Thereafter, both Jobeda and her sea Quaiyum mortgaged their respective shares to Alfazuddin, predecessor-in-interest of defendants-appellants Nos. 1 to 7 by two separate Deeds of Mortgage dated 22 October 1935. The mortgage was followed by sale to the mortgagee under two registered Sale-deeds one dated 10 August 1938 and the other dated 12 April 1939. Since then Alfazuddin possessed the joint property as a co-sharer of the plaintiffs. Now inconvenience of joint possession being felt the plaintiffs filed the suit for simple partition to the extent of 5 pakhis 2 gondas. On objection hazing been raised the plaint was amended and a prayer far establishment of title was included in the plaint. 

 24. The suit was resisted by the defendants, who are heirs of Alfazuddin, by a written statement. They totally denied any title of Hedayet Baksh from the very beginning of the kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920. Their case is that the settlement under the kabuliyat was taken by Jobeda alone with her own money and for her own benefit and interest, but Hedayet Baksh who was brother of Jobeda's husband and was brought to her house to look after her affairs on her husband's death, fraudulently got his name inserted in the kabuliyat. That is why Hedayet was not recognized as a tenant by the landlord nor his name was mutated in the landlord's Sherista nor did he possess the land nor paid any rent but jobeda alone possessed the entire land and paid rent first to the landlord and then to the Government after State Acquisition. By the two Mortgage-deeds (as referred to above) Jobeda and her son Quaiyum, had first mortgaged the entire suit land to Alfazuddin and thereafter sold the entire land to him by two registered Sale-deeds whereupon Alfazudditn who was a stranger, entered into possession as owner and possessed it all through openly in assertion of his own title to the exclusion of the plaintiffs and others including Hedayet's brother Rahat and sister Jarina; from the date of settlement in 1920 till the filing of the suit in 1968 no claim of partition or for any usufruct of the land was made by Hedayet and after his death by his heirs, the plaintiffs; the suit was filed malafide as a test case for grabbing the property; the suit was barred by limitation. 

 24A. Plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses but adduced no documentary evidence except the admitted kabuliyat dated 2 June 1920 (Ext 1). Defendants examined 4 witnesses and produced a number of documents including seven registered Barga-kabutiyats, 18 Rent receipts and some khatians besides the undisputed Mortgage Deeds and Sale Deeds in favour of Alfazuddin. On consideration of these materials the trial Court found that except Hedayet's name appearing in the kabuliyat, Ext 1, there is no evidence whatever that he took settlement of the land along with Jobeda, that Hedayet was neither recognized as a tenant by the landlord nor did he pay any rent nor did he participate in any usufruct of the land and that it is Jobeda who alone possessed the land allthrough till she and her son transferred the entire suit land first by mortgage and then by out-right sale to Alfazuddin. The trial Court further found that Alfazuddin possessed the entire land to the exclusion of the plaintiffs claiming title for himself and that even if Hedayet had originally got any title to the extent of 6 ½   pakhis under the kabuliyat. Ext. 1, his title was extinguished by adverse possession of Jobeda and her transferee. On appeal, the learned District Jude reversed these findings and held that Hedayet had got his title to the extent of 6 ½  pakhis under the kabuliyat and possessed the land jointly with Jobeda and after transfer of the land to Alfazuddin, me plaintiff's possessed the land through Alfazuddin who was their co-sharer whose possession was not adverse to the plaintiffs. This finding bas been concurred in by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division against whose decision this appeal has been preferred as already stated in the judgment of my learned brother B.H. Chowdhury. J. 

 25. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Advocate for the defendants- appellants, has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Single Judge rejecting the appellants contention of adverse possession from the beginning of the settlement, more particularly from 1935 when Jobeda and her son mortgaged the entire land to Alfazuddin, a stranger. The learned Counsel does not dispute the general principle of law that possession of a co-sharer in a joint property is possession on behalf of other co-sharers as well and that joint possession Continues till other co-sharers are completely ousted by exclusive possession in assertion or hostile title, publicly and openly for a period of 12 years; but he contends that the position is quite different in the instant case where a stranger entered into possession on the claim of exclusive title for the whole of the property. The possession of such a stranger transferee, the learned counsel contends, is adverse light from the beginning who in fact is not a co-sharer. As to knowledge of the co-owners about adverse possession, the learned Counsel contends that it is not necessary that the person claiming adverse possession on claim of hostile title should bring the matter to the knowledge of his transferor's co-sharers but it is sufficient that he possessed the land openly without any attempt to conceal it from the co-sharers and that he possessed it on claim of his exclusive title, The learned Counsel further contends that even if the stranger purchaser's title was defective or invalid still it does not matter so far as his possession is concerned and that the adverse possession begins right from his entry into possession. In the instant case the learned Counsel contends, the plaintiffs were fully aware of the defendants  possession on claim of title of the whole of the suit land. 

 26. Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents, has stoutly defended the High Court Division's decision and contended that Alfazuddin by entering into possession of the suit land became a co-sharer with the plaintiffs no matter his sale-deeds evidenced transfer to him of the entire ejmali land; the sale-deeds are invalid to the extent of the plaintiff's share and as such they continued to be co-sharers in the joint property and that joint-possession shall be presumed to continue till the defendants prove complete ouster of the plaintiffs by adverse possession for 12 years. The learned Counsel has pointed out that plaintiffs predecessor Hedayet, had acquired title in the suit land to the extent of 6½  pakhis ad that this title could not have been extinguished except upon complete ouster on claim of hostile title a case which was not established by the defendants in this suit. 

 27. As it appears clearly, a. review of the evidence is necessary to determine the real question involved in this appeal, particularly when it centres found loss of title by adverse possession which is itself mixed question of law and fact. The first  point is whether Hedayet had acquired any title by kabuliyat Ext. 1 dated 2-6-1920 A.D. on the face of it he did acquire 6 ½  pakhis along with Jobeda Khatun Whose share was 13 ½  pakhis; whereas defendants totally denied such title, Widow of Hedayet (P.W.3) is one of the plaintiff. In her deposition she claimed that her husband had paid salami and acquired his interest under the kabuliyat but regarding the sources of salami or whether her husband got any means to procure this money she did not say anything. On the other hand, evidence adduced by both D.W. 1. son of Alfazuddin and P.W.1, son-in-law of P.W.3 read along with pleadings of both the parties, clearly shows that Hedayet (brother of Jobeda's husband) bad neither any land nor any house of his own that whatever ancestral landed property he had lie sold it away and resided in the house of Jobeda and after his exit. from that house he lived in the house of his father-in-law in a different village, Zinjira, a few miles away from Jobeda's village in which the suit-bud was situated. Jobeda on the other hand got sufficient resources both from her father and her late previous husband and that at her request Hedayet lived in her house from where he was driven out by her. This claim of the defendants in the written statement has not been disputed. Therefore evidence on record does not give any indication about Hedayet's means to pay for the salami, Be that as it may for the sake of argument I would take that he had paid the salami for his share and acquired title to the extent of 6½  pakhis of the property. But us to possession, evidence of P.W.3 is that Hedayet possessed his share jointly with Jobeda. Such possession, even if accepted continued only for a year or two, for he left the village Kaliganj where the land lay and settled in Zinjira from where he could have possessed only through Jobeda, But admitted fact is that his name was not mutated in the landlord's Sherista nor did he pay any rent nor his name was recorded in the Petty Settlement khatian Ext D (1) which was published some time in 1933. Ext. D(1) recorded Jobeda's name as owner in-possession to the extent of 13 ½  Pakhis in one of the two khatians, The trial Court held that non-participation in any profits from the land, non-payment of any rent and non-recording of his name either in tile landlord's sherista or In any record-of-rights showed that he got no title in the land tinder the kabuliyat which was not acted upon in his case. But the appellate Court took the view that since Hedayet was a co-sharer under the kabuliyat non-participation in profits or non-payment of rent would not extinguish his title. This is true, hut if Jobeda's title was hostile from the very beginning, then by her adverse possession Hedayet's title had extinguished by the time he died, I shall, however not take this view as Hedayet's name appeared in the kabuliyat and presume that he was  a co-sharer of Jobeda with or through whom he possessed his share and that the joint possession continued even after his death and see the subsequent development. 

 28. There is no dispute that Jobeda and her son Quaiyum transferred their entire interests first by mortgage in 1935 and then by sale in 1938-39 to AIfazuddin a stranger. Under these documents Alfazuddin entered into possession of the entire land asserting title over it and if this fact was known to Hedayet's heirs, then Alfazuddin's possession became adverse from the date of his entry into possession. The learned District Judge took the view that for adverse possession it must be brought to the notice of co-sharers and that in this case there was no evidence of such knowledge. This observation is not correct for besides these plaintiffs (who are two daughters and the widow), Hedayet left one brother Rabat Baksh and one sister Jarina as his heirs. Rahat Baksh and Jarina never claimed any share in the land as co-sharer of Alfazuddin. On the contrary Rahat Baksh was a witness to the Sale-deeds, Ext. E and E(1), by which Alfazuddin purchased the entire suit, land including his (Rahat) own interest, if any, therein. The learned District Judge observed that Rahat had married Alfazuddin sister and as such he intentionally kept the matter concealed from the plaintiffs acting in collusion with Alfazuddin. This observation is based on mare conjecture. For no where in the plaint or in the evidence the plaintiffs took such a plea that Rahat had married Alfazuddin's sister and acted in collusion with Alfazuddin or that he bad intentionally suppressed the fact of transfer of the land. Rather P.W. 2. Firoza one of the two daughters of Hedayet sated that her uncle Rahat  Baksh "used to maintain us "Rahat was a government servant and understood the implication  of the transfer to the entire suit land to a stranger under Sale-Deeds. His interest in the land  as common with the plaintiffs interest and he had no reason to keep the transfer suppressed. It is D.W. 1, son of Alfazuddin, who asked whether Rahat had married his father's sister and his answer was in the affirmative. But even if Rabat had married Alfazuddin's sister, there is no evidence that the marriage took place before this transaction, for if he had married after he attested the Transfer Deed then he had no reason to suppress it. In the absence of any plea taken by the plaintiffs, the learned District Judge went off the track to make out a case as to suppression of fact by Rahat. 

 32. Another piece of evidence of defendants possession is seven registered Barga Kabuliyats, Ext. B series. Evidence of D.W. 1. which is supported by P.W. 4, is that his father possessed the land though different bargaders. He produced these Barga Kabuliyats Executed by the respective Borgaders over a period of 25 years, the first one being dated 2-6-36 and the last one being dated 4-4-02. These bargaders delivered adhi-share not to the plaintiffs but to Alfazuddin alone. We find no basis for the observation of the learned District Judge that these Barga Kabuliyats might have been created for the purpose or fabricating evidence of title. 

 33. From the evidence discussed above, I find two distinct stages of possession of the laud, first one from 1920 to 1934 that is, from the date of Kabuliyat Ext. 1 till the death of Hedayet, and the second one from the time of Hedayet's death till the filing of the suit in 1968, more particularly from transfer of the land to Alfazuddin in 1935. For the sake of argument I would accept that Hedayet was a co-sharer under Ext. 1 in 1920 and also that he was in constructive possession of his share through Jobeda and then see whether the law of adverse possession came in operation against his heirs from 1935 when Alfazuddin, a stranger, on claim of 16-annas title, began to possess the  land alone. A co-sharer's possession is possession on behalf of all co-sharers and this possession is presumed to continue till other co-sharers are ousted completely by exclusive possession openly on claim of hostile title by another co-sharer. This principle of law was propounded by the Judicial Committee of tile Privy Council in the case of Corea Vs. Apuhamy AIR 1914 PC 243, in which Lord Macnaughten cited the dictum of V.C. Wood In Thomas vs. Thomas that possession is never considered adverse if it is referred to a lawful title. Similar view had been expressed  much earlier by Lord ,Denman C.J. in Culley  v. Doe Dem Taylerson. 11A & E. 1008 (1840) in the following terms: 

 Mr. Khondaar Mahbubuddin Ahmed argued that in spite of Alfazuddin's Mortgage-Deeds and Sale-Deeds showing transfer of the whole of the land to him, plaintiffs share remained unaffected and they continued as co-sharers of Alfazuddin and as such it is only their complete ouster, the onus of which lies on the defendants, that their title could be lost by adverse possession. 

 35. In support of their respective contentions the learned counsels cited a great number of decision. In Bhavrdo  v. Rakhmin,  23 Bom 137 (F.B.), some co-parceners of a joint family estate alienated  by mortgage and safe "certain defined and distinct portions" of the joint estate to a stranger who began possession claiming exclusive title. In a suit for partition by other co-perceners the plea of adverse possession taken by the alignee  was accepted by the court. In that case Article 127 of the Limitation Act was not held applicable as this Article applies only in cases between the members of a joint family and net to the case of a stranger in whose case Article 144 applies. As to the purchaser's possession it was held : 

 "The answer, we think, must be than as he enters as owner and in right of his conveyance, his possession is adverse to them also. In the eve of law, all the co-parceners though for the sake of convenience they may be in separate possession of portions of the joint estate, are the owners of the whole estate including the alienaled portion. It may be and indeed is the case that such a purchaser by his purchase does not get a good title to the land conveyed to him by a Sink co-parcener, but only the qualified right laid down in Pardurang v. Bhaskar (supra), and he is liable under some circumstances even to be evicted if the co-parceners take the requisite steps within the statutory period Nevertheless, his exclusive possession does not en that account case to be adverse. He, entering as owner, his possession must, we think, necessarily be adverse to the true owners. Adverse possession depends upon the claim to title under which the possessor holds and not upon a consideration of the question in whom the true ownership is vested whether in a single person or in many jointly." 

 "To constitute a plaintiff's title by adverse possession, the possession required to be proved must be adequate in continuity, in publicity, and in extent, and is displaced by evidence of partial possession by the defendant," 

 Mr. Pal contends that the defendants case fully fits into this principle as laid down and fulfills all the requirements of acquisition of title by adverse possession. In the case before us the principle as to acquisition of title by adverse possession has not been invoked by the plaintiffs, but it has been invoked by the defendants to maintain their possession under mortgage-deeds followed by sale-deeds for over a period of 30 years, a possession which was open without any concealment and in the exercise of hostile title. 

 38. The next case relied upon by Mr. Pal is Bharat Pillai V. Jeebarahmal, 46 IA, PC 285. There, possession of one co-shares was held to be adverse against the other co-sharer of a joint property. The Judicial Committee took note of the general principle that one tenant in common could not maintain an ejectment suit against another tenant in common in ordinary circumstances bra, the Committee held, where the letter tenant had not been in participation of rent and profits for a condonable length of time and other circumstances concurred then the court should hold ouster 'of the latter tenant. Mr. Pal has tried to reinforce his argument that if a stranger enters upon possession of any ejmali property either in whole or in part under any conveyance executed by one of several co sharers, then though the conveyance is invalid the stranger's possession is adverse right from the beginning and this possession ripens into title on the expiry of the statutory period of 12 years. In Lala Hem Chand V. Lala Peary Lal and others, AIR 1942, PC 64, a defendant claimed title by adverse possession on the basis of a trust which was held to be void on the ground of vagueness as to its contents. The plaintiffs' suit for ejectment was dismissed and it was held: 

 40. Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed, as already state above, does not agree that a stranger purchasing the whole of an ejmali property is not a co-sharer. He contends that such a purchaser, whether he purchases whole of the ejmali property or any share thereof, is also a co-sharer and his possession is governed by the general principle that a co-sharer's possession is possession on behalf of all other co-sharers. He has referred to the case of Muzaffar Khan Vs. Yousuf Khan., PLD (1959) . SC 9. in which the vendee of a co-sharer of an undivided property was held to be a co-sharer and is entitled to pre-emption under the North Western Frontier Province Preemption Act. Balaram Vs. Shyamcharan, 24 CWN 1057, a similar question arose for determination by the Calcutta High Court and it was held that the possession of land, under common title, of one co-owner would not be presumed to be adverse to other co-sharers but ordinarily, it could be held for the benefit of all. It was observed : 

 "The law will never construe a possession tortious, unless from necessity : on the other hand its gill consider every possession lawful the commencement and continuance of which is not proved to be wrongful and this, upon the principle that every man shall be presumed to act in obedience to his duty, until the contrary appears. In other words, the only difference between the possess slots of a co-owner and other cases is, that acts, which, if done, by a stranger, would perse be a disseisin, are, in the case of tenancies in common,  susceptible of explanation consistently with the real title acts of ownership are not, in tenancies in common, acts of disseisin; it depends upon the intent with winch they are done and their notoriety; the law will not presume that cue tenant in common intends to oust another; the facts must be notorious and the intent must be established in proof." 

 Facts in this case are that the property belonged to three brothers two of whom had left their ancestral home in the village and settled in another village and were not in possession for 50 years; during this period their brother who stayed back possessed the hind paying rent alone in his name, and dealt with the entire properly as his own and then transferred it to the defendant, a stronger. Plaintiffs purchased 2/3rd share from these two absentee brothers and filed a suit for partition on declaration of title. The defendant pleaded adverse possession as a stranger purchaser, but the contention was rejected on the ground that he became a co-sharer in the land and his possession was on behalf of other two co-sharers and that his possession did not exclude them. 

 41. The next case relied upon by Kh. Mahbubuddin Ahmed is Izat Baksh Sarkar v. Abdul Quadir Bhuiyan, 21 DLR (SC) 444. In that case a brother sold certain property to a stranger claiming the property as his own, whereas it belonged to him and his two minor brothers. The purchaser possessed the property openly, exclusively and in assertion of his own title or mutation of his name and by payment of rent. The minors took no step to assert their title for long 21 years even, after they attained majority. In that case the general rule that a co-sharers possession is possession on behalf of other co-sharers was applied and the plea of adverse possession was rejected, The Court, however, observed that this does not mean that a co-sharer can never possess adversely to the other co-sharers and acquire title by adverse possession. To enable one of the co-sharers to acquire title by adverse possession as against the other co-sharers, his possession must be of such an actual, open, notorious, exclusive and hostile character as to amount to an ouster or exclusion of the other co-sharers. Moreover, such possession must be for a continuous period of at least 12 years in assertion of a hostile title to the knowledge of the co-sharers against whom title by adverse possession is claimed. Such knowledge may be proved directly or inferentially," It may be noted that in both these cases original title of the contending co-sharers was not in dispute and that they got the property by inheritance; whereas in the instant case the original title of the plaintiffs predecessor, Hedayet, is in dispute. Kh. Mahbubuddin has also relied upon the following cases where the same principle as to a co sharer's possession has been re-stated and applied. Maroon Mia v. Majiduddin, 4 DLR 114; Bindhu Bala v. Rabati Mohan, 4 DLR 293, Maharaja Bhupendra Singh v. Sudhindra Chandra Singh, 5 DLR 251; Abdul Jalil Shikder  v. Khurshed Ali, 27 DLR AD 143, and & Mohar Ali v. Zafar Ali, 27 DLR 451. 

 "Adverse possession must be within the knowledge of the co-sharer; mere possession by mortgagee from the co-owner does not amount to ouster. A co-owner has no duty cast upon him to watch the conduct of another co-owner and be on lookout to find out the extent of the share purported to be transferred by him and to intervene if more than the real shave has been transferred. He is entitled to assume that the permissive nature of Vie possession has passed on to his co-owner's transferee who has now become the co-owner in place of the original co-owner. Of course if the assertion of title to the whole is brought to his knowledge and it is accompanied by his ouster and exclusion, adverse possession would then commence as against him". The minority view was, however, that "a mortgage of the entire property by one of the proprietors is a clear assertion of adverse title and the possession of the mortgagee is surely adverse to the co-owners of the mortgagors." 

 42. Now coming back to the instant case, the position of Alfazuddin as I find was that of a trespasser from 1935 if Hedayet had acquired title to the extent of 6 ½  pakhis under the kabuliyat. This was so because Alfazuddin entered into possession of the whole of land on claim of 16-annas title under his title deeds which were invalid to the extent of the plaintiffs share. But whether Alfazuddin entered into possession as a trespasser or as plaintiffs co-sharer, his exclusive possession exercised openly on claim of 16 annas title constituted complete ouster of the plaintiffs; and this possession is certainly adverse and has over the period of 33 years extinguished whatever title the plaintiffs had in the land. This adverse possession was very much within the knowledge of the plaintiffs from the time of this entry into the land. from 1935. This knowledge is clearly established from paragraph 3 of their plaint and also from their total unconcern about the land. As to the knowledge of their co-sharer Rabat Baksh about the transfer, since his interest in the land was common with theirs, there was no season why he would not disclose the matter to them. By the Sale deeds he attested his own interest also was transferred, if he had any. Possession on Alfazadnin was open, in total exclusion of the plaintiffs, on claim of title and without any attempt at concealment over this long period during which plaintiffs had no participation in profits of the land or payment of rent; their names were not recorded in any document nor did they ever claim any benefit from or partition of this land. In fact they had no connection with the land from 1935, and nothing was known about them till they filed the suit, according to the defendants, just to take a chance to establish title. The suit is hopelessly barred under Article 144 of the Limitation Act. Views taken by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division tend to show that once a co-sharer always a co-sharer and that against a co-sharer there can be no extinguishment of title by adverse possession. Plaintiff and before them, their predecessor were completely out of scene from the date of the kabuliyat. In these circumstances, the suit was rightly dismissed by the trial Court.
justice_names: Mr. Justice F. K. M. Abdul Munim

parties:
Rezia Khatun and others -------- Plaintiff—opposite party ...petitioners
-Vs-
Jahangir Hossain and others --------- Defendant -petitioner opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Soumendra Sarker, J.:- The Rule issued calling upon the Opposite Party No.1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 01.12.2016 passed by the learned District Judge, Patuakhali in Civil 'Revision No.66 of 2015 allowing the same and setting aside the judgment and order dated 19.11.2015 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No.99 of 1979 allowing the application under Order VI, rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint and another application under section 151 read with section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.99 of 1979 should not be set aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule in a nutshell can be stated thus, the present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted the original Title Suit being No.99 of 1979 in the Court of learned the then Sub-ordinate Judge, Patuakhali for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession contending inter alia that the land appertaining to Mouza Dabluganj of Kolapara police station under Patuakhali District in khatian No.295 measuring an area 9.88 acres originally belonged to one Arob Ali Sarder. Arob Ali died leaving behind two sons namely Kashem Ali and Najem Ali. Najem Ali transferred his 08 annas share in favour of one Abdul Motaleb, the predecessor of the plaintiff-petitioners by a registered kabala deed dated 16.02.1940 and the possession was delivered in favour of the purchaser. The original kabala deed of the plaintiffs was lost due to devastating cyclone in the year 1943 and taking advantage of that; Kashem Ali and Najem Ali with an ill-intention managed to get their names recorded in R.S. and S.A. khatians. After the death of Abdul Motaleb, the plaintiffs being his only heirs possessing the suit land. The defendants while threatened the plaintiffs; the plaintiffs instituted the original suit. 

 3. The contrary case of the contesting defendants No.1-3 in short is thus, that the suit land originally belonged to Kashem Ali, who did never transfer the land in favour of the predecessor of the plaintiffs. The plaintiff's predecessor only to grab the property created a forged document. The further case of the defendants is such that the plaintiffs have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. The defendants alleged that the original owner Arab Ali Sarder had two sons namely Kashem Ali and Najem Ali. Kashem Ali died unmarried leaving behind his only brother Najem Ali and after the death of Najem Ali his heirs are possessing the land. 

 4. During trial of the original suit the learned trial court after taking evidence from the sides of the respective parties, decreed the suit on contest by his judgment and decree dated 30.11.1985 and 07.12.1985 respectively. Subsequent to that judgment and decree, while the plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the suit property; they came to learn that a mistake has been committed by their engaged the then lawyer; in the plaint of the original suit and instead of actual R.S. plot No.4893 of R.S. khatian No. 296, the learned lawyer at the time of drafting of the plaint inserted R.S. plot No.4891 wrongly. The concerned R.S. khatian No.296 has been exhibited before the learned trial court; from where it is apparent that the R.S. plot is 4893 not 4891. The plaintiffs finding necessity to correct the plot number filed an application before the learned trial court to rectify the aforesaid clerical mistake in the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.99 of 1979 and the learned trial court by its judgment and order dated 19.11.2015 allowed both the applications for amendment of the plaint as well as amendment of the judgment and decree. 

 10. Considering submissions of the learned Advocates, having gone through the order passed by the learned trial court in Title Suit No.99 of 1979 on 19.11.2015 and the impugned judgment and order dated 01.12.2016 passed by the 1st court of revision in Civil Revision No.66 of 2015 along with the relevant R.S. and S.A. khatians with the certified copes of plaint, judgment and decree, applications for amendment of the plaint as well as the judgment and decree passed by the trial court dated 07.12.1985 in Title Suit No.99 of 1979, it transpires that after the judgment and decree passed by the trial court in the original Title Suit No.99 of 1979, the learned trial court i.e. the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali received 

 15. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 01.12.2016 passed by the learned District Judge, Patuakhali in Civil Revision No.66 of 2015 allowing the same and setting aside the judgment and order dated 19.11.2015 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Patuakhali in Title Suit No.99 of 1979 allowing the application under Order VI Rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the plaint and another application under section 151 read with section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.99 of 1979 is hereby set aside.

parties:
SMAH Ltd ------ Petitioner 
vs
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in brief, are: The petitioner is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act. Mrs. Madlena D Rozario (since deceased), wife of Ketu Rozario purchased the land appertaining to CS Plot No. 177 of mouza Begunbari, PS Tejgaon, Dhaka measuring an area of 1.25 acres of land from the CS recorded owners by a registered deed of sale dated 12-6-1950. The name of Mrs. Rozario was duly recorded both in SA and RS khatiansin respect of that land. The Government by an order dated 3-3-1952 requisitioned the land under section 30f the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) and included the same in LA Case No. 16 of 1959-60 for the purpose of cutting earth for the Railway Department. The land was subsequently de-requisitioned, released and restored to Mrs Madlena D Rozario by issuing a notice under Rule 10(2) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 issued under the joint signatures of the Additional Land Acquisition Collector, Dhaka and the Additional District Magistrate, Dhaka Despite the release and restoration of possession of the land to the original owner, the same was included in the list of enemy property in the Tejgaon Police Station VP Case No. 566 of 1968 at the behest of certain interested quarters. For proper utilisation and management including power to sell off the land, Mrs. Rozario executed and registered a general power of attorney in favour of her son, Jacob Rozario and one Edward Purification on 14-1-1986. The attorneys of the original owner entered into a contract with Md Saifur Rahman Khan on 14-1-1986 to sell 0.18 acre of land and delivered possession thereof to him. Since the attorneys refused to execute and register the deed of sale, Md Saifur Rahman Khan instituted a suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 in the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka. The suit was decreed by judgment and decree dated 15-8-1988 (Annexure-E). During pendency of the suit, the then Martial Law Government issued Martial Law Order (MLO) No. 128 dated 13-5-1986 which was published in the official Gazette on 20-5-1986 cancelling all previous letters, orders as if they had never been issued in respect of the lands acquired by erstwhile Government of East Pakistan under LA Case No. 66 of 1957-1958. LA Case No. 16/1959-1960 was also included in the schedule to that MLO for the construction of Dhaka Tongi Diversion Road. By the MLO all the previous letters, orders and instruments were cancelled and re-vested the properties described in the schedule of the MLO to the Government. The legal heirs of Mrs Rozario in compliance with the decree executed a deed of sale dated 30-9-1989 in favour of the petitioner's vendor, Md Saifur Rahman Khan. Thereafter, the attorneys of the original owner also executed a deed of exchange and transferred more land in favour of the petitioner's vendor. In this way the petitioner's vendor became owner of 0.19 acre of land appertaining to CS Plot No. 177 of Begunbari Mouza, Tejgaon, Dhaka. Since the land was released in favour of Mrs. Rozario, she made a series of applications to the different authorities including the vested property authority for release and restoration of the disputed land. Accordingly, the land was released from the list of vested property and ultimately, it was restored to the original owner. Respondent No.6, the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka filed a suit being Title Suit No. 28 of 1992 in the 3rd Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Dhaka seeking declaration that the decree dated 15-8-1988 (Annexure-E) passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 and the deed of exchange dated 3-6-1989 were illegal and inoperative, and also sought for recovery of khas possession. The plaint of the suit was rejected on a contested hearing by judgment and order dated 16-5-1996 against which the Government did not prefer any appeal. Respondent No.2 issued letter dated 18-7-1993 and allotted 5 kathas of land which is the petitioner's land treating the same as industrial plot No. 30 in favour of respondent No.8, Habib Hotel International Limited but did not hand over possession thereof. The petitioner purchased 5 kathas of land from Md Saifur Rahman Khan on payment of valuable consideration and got registration of the deed of sale bearing No. 1752 dated 2-5-1996. The name of the petitioner was mutated in respect of that 5 kathas of land in Miscellaneous Case No. 144 of 1998 dated 6-10-1998. The Government recently carried out a survey in which the name of the petitioner was duly recorded. After a long lapse of 10 years of allotment, respondent No.2 executed and registered a deed of lease dated 9-10-2002 in favour of respondent No.8 but could not deliver possession thereof. When the respondents threatened to dispossess the petitioner from his purchased land, he filed a suit being Title Suit No. 189 of 2003 in the 2nd Court of the Assistant Judge, Dhaka for permanent injunction. On an application filed by the petitioner, the trial Court passed an ad-interim order directing the parties to maintain status quo which was made absolute on 21-6-2003. On an appeal by the respondents, the order of status quo was stayed on 28-6-2003. in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 175 of 2003 respondent No. 2 issued a letter dated 26-5-2003 directing the Executive Engineer, Public Works Division 3, Segunbagicha, Dhaka to arrange for handing over possession of the disputed land to respondent No.8. The respondents unilaterally obtained an order on 3-6-2003 setting aside the mutation and deleting the petitioner's name from the record of right. When it came to the knowledge of the petitioner, it filed an appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 65 of 2003 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka and obtained an order of stay on 22-6-2003. 

 4. Respondent No. 2 filed an affidavit- in-opposition controverting the material allegations made in the Writ Petition. The case of respondent No.2, in short, is that the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 of CS Khatian No. 49 along with other lands of different plots of that mouza was requisitioned by the Government by the order dated 28-9-1959 and 25-2-1960 under section 3 of the Act and those lands continued to be subject matter of requisition. Subsequently, the requisitioned lands were acquired by the Government and accordingly, a Gazette notification was published on 28-3-1968. Therefore, the land vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and the right, title and interest of the original owner in those lands were extinguished. By MLO 128 of 1986 acquisition of the land in question was reconfirmed. The Senior Sub-Assistant Engineer, Bangladesh Railway had no authority to write any letter dated 20-9-1986 to the Executive Engineer to de-requisition the property. The letter dated 20-9- 1986 (Annexure-H) is collusive, concocted and manufactured to grab the land of the Government. The land of CS Plot No. 177 having not been treated as vested property, the question of release of the same in pursuance of Annexure-H series does not arise. 

 5. Respondent No. 8 also filed an affidavit- in-opposition. The case of respondent No.8 is the same as that of respondent No.2. Respondent No. 9 also filed an affidavit-in-opposition. The case of respondent No. 9 is that the land of the disputed plot along with other lands was acquired for Railway. Therefore, it is not relevant for which purposes the land is used by the Railway Department. The Railway Department was not made a party in Title Suit No, 84 of 1988 and it was not aware of the decree passed in that suit. In MLO No. 128 of 1986, only a schedule had been given to show the acquired land to be used for Tongi Diversion Road. It does not affect, curtail or extinguish the title and ownership of Bangladesh Railway over the land acquired in LA Case No. 16 of 1959-1960. The contents, prayers and outcome of Title Suit No. 28 of 1992 and Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 do not curtail, affect or extinguish the right, title or ownership of the Railway Department over the disputed land. 

 6. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that by MLO No. 128 of 1986 the Government acquired 1.04 acres of land from the disputed CS Plot No. 177 and that the rest of the land of that plot remained with the original owner Mrs Madlena D Rozario and, as such, the petitioner acquired valid right, title and interest in respect of 0.19 acre of land of CS Plot No. 177 on the basis of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 for specific performance of contract. He further submits that for setting aside the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract, the Government filed Title Suit No.5 of 1983 and that the plaint of that suit was rejected. He continues that since rejection of plaint amounts to decree and since the Court found that the petitioner acquired valid title in respect of 0.19 acre of land, the Government subsequently cannot lease out any portion of that land to respondent No.8. Mr TH Khan lastly submits that so long the decree passed in Title Suit No. 5 of 1983 is in existence, the Government cannot claim any right, title and possession in respect of any land of CS Plot No. 177. 

 7. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed along with Mr KZ Alam, learned Advocates, appeared on behalf of respondent No.8. Mr Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that after publication of the notification in the official Gazette the right, title and interest of the original owner, Mrs Madlena D. Rozario was extinguished in respect of CS Plot No. 177 and that the decree passed in the subsequent suit will not confer any title on the original owner and that the subsequent purchaser (the petitioner) will not acquire any right, title, interest or possession in the land of CS Plot No. 177. He further submits that MLO No.148 of 1986 deals with LA Case No. 66/1957-1958 and that part of the land of CS Plot No. 177 was shown in the schedule to that MLO for the purpose of showing the actual land required for Dhaka- Tongi Diversion Road and, as such, the MLO does not have any bearing on LA Case No. 16/1959-1960. 

 8. Mr AHM Mushfiqur Rahman, learned Assistant Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of respondent No.2, submits that since the disputed land of CS Plot No.177 was acquired on the basis of Gazette notification dated 28-3-1968, it absolutely vested in the Government free from all encumbrances and, as such, the petitioner cannot derive any title on the basis of the decree passed in the two suits. 

 10. Admittedly, the disputed CS Plot No. 177 measuring an area of 1.25 acres of land appertaining to CS Khatian No. 49 (Annexure-R to the supplementary affidavit) belonged to Mrs. Madlena D. Rozario as evident from Annexure-Q, the deed of sale No. 2727 dated 2-6-1950. The petitioner admits that the land of the disputed plot was requisitioned in LA Case No. 16/1959-1960. The petitioner, however, "contends that the Government issued a notice (Annexure-C) under Rule 2) of the (Emergency), Requisition of Property Rules, 1948 for release and restoration of the requisitioned property. According to the petitioner, possession of that property was delivered to the original owner on 18-1-1960. A perusal of Annexure-C reveals that on 3-3-1952 the land of the disputed plot No. 177 was requisitioned on 3-3-1952, which the petitioner also admits in its Writ Petition. It is not comprehensible how the disputed property could be requisitioned when the LA. Case itself was started in 1959-1960. Annexure C also does not contain any date of issue of notice and as such, the very genuineness of Annexure-C is doubtful. Annexure-B, the official gazette dated 28-3-1968 filed with the affidavit-in-reply of the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No.2, reveals that the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 along with the lands of other plots was acquired. The relevant portion of the Gazette notification is quoted below: 

 11. After publication of the Gazette notification the title of the original owner Mrs Madlena D Rozario was extinguished once and for all in the entire CS Plot No. 177. 

 13. We find substantial force in the submission of Mr. Ahmed. We are, however, of the view that by MLO No. 128 of 1986, the title of Mrs Madlena D Rozario was, not restored in 0.29 acre of land of CS Plot No. 177 after deduction of 1.04 acres of land required for Dhaka- Tongi Diversion Road because her title vested in the Government as per the Gazette, notification dated 28-3-1968. Therefore, Annexure-F is of no avail to the petitioner, Annexure-'D' to the Writ Petition reveals that Mrs Madlena D. Rozario executed and registered a general power of attorney on 14-1-1986 in favour of Edward Purification and her son Jacob Rozario empowering them to do all acts including sale in respect of the land of entire CS Plot Nos 163 and 177 corresponding to SA Plot Nos. 286 and 310 and RS Plot Nos. 5126 and 5121 measuring 1.23 acres of land. On the date of execution of the power of attorney, the attorneys entered into a contract with Md Saifur Rahman Khan to sell 0.19 acre of land of CS Plot No. 177. Md Saifur Rahman Khan, thereafter, filed a suit for specific performance of contract being Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 which was decreed on 15-8-1988, The petitioner is relying on' both Annexures-F and D. When 1.04 acres of land of CS Plot No. 177 were taken away by MLO No. 128 of 1986 (Annexure-F), it is not comprehensible how the original owner could appoint attorneys in respect of the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 and this has not been explained by the petitioner. It is remarkable to note that the date on which the two attorneys entered into a contract with Md Saifur Rahman Khan, the original owner (Mrs Madlena D Rozario) registered the power of attorney in favour of the attorneys. Therefore, the original owner herself could enter into the contract instead of her attorneys. Before the obtaining of the decree by Md Saifur Rahman Khan in the suit for specific performance of contract in respect of 0.19 acres of land of CS Plot No. 177, the entire land of that plot vested in the Government free from all encumbrances by the Gazette notification dated 28-3-1968. As such, the petitioner by its alleged purchase from Md Saifur Rahman Khan has not acquired any title in respect of 0.19 acre of land of cs Plot No. 177 on the basis of the decree dated 15-8-1988 passed in the suit for specific performance of contract because the title of Mrs Madlena D Rozario in 'that plot was extinguished on 28-3-1968. It is, of course, true that the Government was a party in the suit for specific performance of contract and that the Government failed to contest the suit. When the original owner, Mrs Madlena D Rozario had no title in the land of CS Plot No. 177, it is immaterial whether the Government contested the suit or not. 

 14. Annexure 1 to the Writ Petition shows that the Government filed Title Suit No. 5 of 1993 for setting aside the decree passed in Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 for specific performance of contract. The plaint of Title Suit No. 5 of 1993 was rejected by the Court on 16-5-1996. Mr TH Khan submits that since the rejection of plaint amounts to decree, the Government is bound by the decree passed in Title Suit No. 5 of 1993. We have already found that the petitioner has not acquired any title in the disputed land by the decree passed in Title Suit No, 84 of 1988 and, as such, the decree passed in Title Suit No.5 of 1993 is of no avail to the petitioner. 

 15. Annexure 'H' to the Writ Petition reveals that the entire land of CS Plot No. 177 vested in the Government and that the Government decided to release the same to the original owner Mrs Madlena D Rozario. Annexure 'H2' reveals that the land of the disputed plot was released from the list of vested property. Annexure-'H (6)' reveals that the possession of the entire land of the disputed plot measuring 1.23 (1.25) acres was restored to Abdus Sobhan Miah and others, the vendees of Mrs Madlena D Rozario. It is not comprehensible how the property acquired by the Government on 28-3-1968 was declared vested and even if the property was declared vested before publication of the Gazette notification dated 2S-3-1968, the property of a Christian lady could not be declared vested. Therefore, we find that Annexure-H (series) are mere paper transaction having no legal value. Therefore, the petitioner by its alleged purchase dated 30-4-1995 has not derived any interest in the land of CS Plot No. 177. 

 17. In the case referred to above, the decree was under challenge but here the decrees passed in the two suits, namely, Title Suit No. 84 of 1988 and Title Suit No.5 of 1993 were not under challenge even then the principle enunciated in the case referred to above applies in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 20. In the instant case, we find that the Gazette notification vesting the disputed land in the Government was published on 18-3-1968 which was not cancelled by MLO No. 128 of 1986 and; as such, there is no scope to return the property to the original owner or any person claiming under him.

parties:
Amulya Ratan Chowdhury & others ------ Appellants
VS.
Sreemati Shaibalini Ghose and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : Plaintiff-Appellants of Civil Appeal No. 48 of 1995 filed Other Suit No. 168 of 1985 against the defendant-respondents in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for a declaration of title to recovery of khas possession in some part and also for confirmation of possession in the rest of the suit land. Defendant-respondent No. 1 Sreemati Shaibalini Ghosh filed SCC suits against the appellants for their eviction as tenants from the suit land originally in the First Court of Munsif, Chittagong which on transfer to the First Court of Subordinate Judge were registered as SCC Suit Nos. 13-17 of 1988. 

 2. Plaintiff-appellants in their suit alleged, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Amar Krishna Chowdhury and others. On 26-3-1936 they let out the suit property to one Protul Kumar Sen by a registered Bharanama for 9(nine) years at a monthly rental of Taka 8.00 ie, Taka 96.00 per year. It was, provided in the agreement that the landlords would take back the possession of the suit property after the expiry of the stipulated period of 9 years but in case of continuing possession by the tenant beyond 9 years the tenant would pay rent at the rate of Taka 20.00 per month. Subsequently one Sadananda Ghose was inducted into possession by the said Protul Kumar Sen as a bharatia and since then Sadananda Ghose had been paying rent for the suit premises to Amar Krishna Chowdhury and his co-sharers, namely, Benode Behari and others. Plaintiffs case further is that, Sadananda Ghose during his lifetime inducted plaintiff Nos. 1, 3, 4 and 5 and the predecessor of plaintiff No. 6, Parul Bala including defendant Nos. 6-21 in the suit property without the permission of the landlords Benode Behari and others as sub-tenants and that when the landlords raised objection Sadananda Ghose informed them that those persons were his own people and he had not sub-let the premises. After the death of Sadananda Ghose his heirs did not pay rent to Benode Behari and others and when the landlords intended to file suit for ejectment against the plaintiffs and others, the plaintiffs accepted Benode Behari and others as their landlords. Thereafter Benode Behari and others proposed to transfer the suit property as in schedule 1 to the plaintiffs which was subsequently purchased by them, namely, the plaintiffs, by registered kabala on 10-11-1984. Plaintiffs No. 1-7 became owners in possession of schedule 1 & 2 properties by further purchase on 2-12-84. Defendants No. 6-21 are in possession of schedule-3 as sub-tenants of Sadananda Chose. These defendants were asked to deliver possession (of schedule 3 land) who, however, denied the plaintiffs title whereupon the plaintiffs served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, terminating the tenancy of the defendants in respect of the said premises and asking them to vacate the same. Upon these averments the plaintiffs filed the suit. 

 7. Admittedly Sadananda Chose, husband of defendant No. 1 entered into possession of the suit premises on the basis of an agreement for sale with PK Sen & Sons Ext. 1(1). The induction of PK Sen by the landlords in the suit property under a registered Bharanama (Ext. 3) in the year 1936 is also admitted. The learned Subordinate Judge, inter alia, found that the predecessor of the defendant had been possessing the suit property adversely within the knowledge of all for more than 40 years and that the plaintiffs obtained some alleged deeds of title from the original owners who had already lost their title over the suit property by such adverse possession. 

 8. It appears that at the hearing of the appeal in the High Court Division a preliminary point was taken on behalf of the defendant-respondents as to the maintain-ability of the plaintiffs suit itself on the ground that since the plaintiffs were admittedly inducted as tenants by Sadananda Chose and subsequently they continued as such under his wife Sreemati Shaibalini Chose, they could not maintain their suit for declaration of title without first surrendering their possession to the defendant from whose predecessor they got possession in the suit property. Reliance was placed for this proposition on Hajee Abdus Sattar vs. Mahiuddin & ors 38 DLR (AD) 97. 

 10. It was argued on behalf of the plaintiff-appellants in the High Court Division that the aforesaid decision 38 DLR (AD) 97 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case as that was a decision in an SCC suit, whereas the present suit by the plaintiffs was one for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession (in 3rd Schedule) and the defendant's SCC suits for eviction of the plaintiffs were tried along with the title suit as a matter of convenience and therefore a decision on the merit as to the plaintiff's title cannot be deferred until surrendering possession as in the cited case. It was also argued that the plaintiffs had purchased paramount title in the suit property from the original landlords and Sadananda Ghose had not acquired or could not acquire any valid title to the property either through Ext. 3 or Ext.1 (1). 

 11. The High Court Division observed that the principle laid down in Hajee Abdus Sattar's case applied more in the present case because PW 1 who deposed for the plaintiffs admitted that they were inducted into possession by Sadananda Ghose after the liberation of Bangladesh and they paid rent to Shaibalini Ghose after the death of Sadananda till August, 1984 and got receipts. The High Court Division also observed that the plaintiffs had filed their title suit after the filing of at least three SCC suits by Shaibalini Chose denying her title and claiming their own title in the suit land therefore "we hold that in view of the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 97 the plaintiffs cannot maintain their suit as it appears to us that this is simply a counter-blast to the proceedings initiated by Shaibalini Ghose against the admitted tenants." 

 13. At the hearing of the leave petitions, Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate for the appellants, submitted that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the suit was not maintainable on the principle of 38 DLR (AD) 97 because in this case the learned Subordinate Judge was considering not only the SCC suits of the defendant but also the title suit of the plaintiffs and the main point that arose on the pleadings of the parties for decision was whether the contesting defendants had acquired title to the suit land by adverse possession and, as such, no question of surrendering/quitting the premises by the plaintiffs arose. 

 14. At the hearing of the appeals, however, Mr. Pal shifted the thrust of his submission and made an attractive argument on the basis of the pleading of the plaintiff-appellants raising a mixed question of law and fact which was neither raised nor considered at any stage heretofore. The argument is that the plaintiffs while in possession of the suit land were threatened with eviction through Court by the landlord Benode Behari Chowdhury and others and the plaintiffs attorned to them and thus they suffered, what is called eviction by title paramount and, as such, the relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the heirs of Sadanada Ghose ceased. The question of surrender before seeking declaration of title therefore does not arise. Mr Pal argued that the Chowdhurys, the original landlords, remained the paramount title-holders because both PK Son and Sadananda Ghosh were lessees in relation to the original landlords. For the purpose of invoking the principle of eviction by title paramount one has to prove that he has been evicted by a third person and that the third person has a paramount title, superior to the title of his alleged lessor. It is not necessary that the person claiming paramount title must in fact evict the person occupying the premises but a threat of eviction only is sufficient to constitute such eviction in the eye of law if the person sought to be evicted attorn to the claimant because the claimant gets in to possession through the lessee who becomes his tenant. Mr. Pal referred to Hallsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 23, paragraph 1213 and the case of Amritalal vs. Uttam Lal, AIR 1939 Calcutta 216 for illustrating the principle of eviction and title paramount. It is true that in the eye of law actual eviction is not necessary and a mere threat of eviction is sufficient to constitute eviction by title paramount if the person sought to be evicted attorn to the claimant of paramount title. 

 15. The question for consideration in this case is whether the plaintiffs have been able to prove that they suffered eviction in the lands of the paramount title-holders, namely, Benode Behari Chowdhury and others as pleaded by them in paragraph 4 of their plaint. It has already been noticed that this plea of eviction by title paramount was argued neither in the trial Court nor in the High Court Division. We have gone through the evidence of PWs 1-5 and found absolutely nothing therein to support the plaintiff's case in the plaint that the original landlords had threatened to evict them from the suit land whereupon they attorned to the said landlords or paid rent to them except that they purchased the suit land when the landlords being in need of money offered to sell it to the plaintiffs. There being no evidence at all in support of the plaintiffs case of attornment to the original landlords the principle of eviction under title paramount which has been sought to be invoked by Mr Pal, although appeared to be attractive, cannot be applied or taken advantage of in the facts and circumstances of the present case. On the other hand, the High Court Division found that it is admitted by the plaintiffs that they were inducted into the suit land by Sadananda Ghosh and they paid rent to him and after his death paid rent to Shaibalini Chose, his wife, until August 1984. The High Court Division has rightly found that the plaintiffs cannot dispute the title of Sadananda Ghosh and his heirs under section 116 of the Evidence Act and in order to claim title to themselves they must surrender the possession of the suit premises in terms of the decision in the case of Haji Abdus Sattar referred to above.
