The plaintiff filed the suit on 8-2-2004 impleading defendant No. 2 Mr. Aktheruzzaman as director of Eastern Housing limited as the attorney of the late Engineer Md. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza wherein the defendant No. 1 is the vendor of plaintiff. So, from the plaint it is crystal clear that Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza defendant No. 1 and Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza the Principal of Eastern Housing Limited is not same and one person. 

 97. Now, if I look into the order sheet of the case record. It appears that after filing the suit on 10-2-2004, 22-2-2004, 18-3-2004 plaintiff took the steps in the suit. On 20-3-2004 in the suit third party by an application under Order I Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure prayed for not substituting the defendant No.1 but for adding as defendants in the suit as the heirs of Engineer Md. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza because of fact that he died on 02-2-2004 and they got the information that instant title suit has been filed by the plaintiff on the basis of the false bainapatra created by him with fictitious person and filed the instant false suit for specific performance of contract having Rio title, interest and possession over the suit property. However, pending aforementioned application of third party plaintiff on 23-3-2004 by filing a fresh Vokalatnama prayed for hearing of the application dated 18-3-2004, upon hearing the application for temporary injunction the Court below issued the show cause notice upon the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why an order of temporary injunction should not be granted. On 27-5-2004 defendant Nos. 1-2 filed hajira. Plaintiff prayed for time, defendant No. 2 by an application under Order-III Rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure prayed for direction upon defendant No. 1 for his personal appearance before the Court. Then the Court below without passing any order regarding personal appearance of the defendant No. 1 on 15-7-2004 allowed the application for added party not as the 3rd party but as the heirs of defendant No. 1. Whereas on that application it has been stated that they are the heirs of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza not the heirs of defendant No. 1 Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur. So, from the record and conduct of the plaintiff it is crystal clear that the defendant No.1 Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur and Engineer Md. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157 Bara Moghbazar is not the same and one person. 

 99. From the above deposition it is further manifest that though plaintiff at the time of filing and sometime after filing of the suit did not admit rather clearly denied existence, right, title and possession of Engineer Md. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar and at the time of his deposition stated that “ইহা সত্য নহে যে মগবাজার নিবাসী শামসুল কবীর হুমায়ুন রেজা অনুমোদিত প্লান মতে ইমারত নির্মান করিয়া ভাড়াটিয়ার মাধ্যমে ভোগদখল করিতেন। but later only to escape and justify his earlier false activities admitted with a device that defendant Nos. 1 (a) to 1(e) are the legal heirs of defendant No. 1 i.e. Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur by substituting but from the above testimony of PW 1 it is manifest that defendant No.1 Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and the father of the defendant Nos. 1(a) to I (e) is not the same and one person. 

 106. In the instant case from the discussions made above I am of the clear opinion that plaintiff not only failed to prove his own case but produced some forged and fabricated deeds and papers because from the facts and circumstances it clear that plaintiff PW 1 produced the exhibit 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in the Court showing his vendor as custodian of those exhibit's who failed to appear before the Court and from the materials on record it is proved that he is none but a fake person. So, exhibit "6" is nothing but obviously the creation of forgery only to grab the suit property. Furthermore, the defence story and facts as set forth are quite believable not only by oral evidences, however, facts and circumstances with possession and documentary evidences, as find support from the testimony of PWs of title suit No.81 of 2006 which has been adopted in this case with the consent of all the parties. 

 108. Now I discuss and consider the appeal from original decree No.327 of 2009 arises which out of title suit No.176 of 2004 filed by living Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. Plaintiff filed the suit against the Rajuk and other official of Rajuk on the following prayers: 

 A. Pass a decree in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants declaring that the plaintiff is legally entitled to get sale permission and the defendants are also bound to issue sale permission in respect of the scheduled property by receiving the proper transfer fees from the plaintiff as per rule of RAJUK. 

 2. Whether the plaintiff has got right, title and possession over the suit land? 

 3. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get the relief as prayed for? 

 113. From the above evidences it appears that the PW 1 though claimed he was a executive engineer but his testimony regarding service book, ACR and Organogram clearly prove that he is not a service holder at all. Not only that when a executive engineer admit that he has no bank account then question is, how he drew his salary which must be paid through A/C payee cheque. Moreover, from his docu-ments which have been exhibited it clearly show that it has been prepared in the name of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of 157 Bara Moghbazar which is admittedly the permanent address of the engineer Shamsul Kabir Huma-yun Reza who is a different person. According to plaint case of title Suit No. 81 of 2006 wherein this plaintiff is the principal defendant No. 3 and contested that suit, now legal question is when other persons claimed the title and filed a title suit impleading this plaintiff as defendant that their father was the real owner and allottee of the same suit plot, then whether present suit simpliciter only for sale permission is maintainable. Especially when both the suits tried and heard by the same Judge simulta-neously and the suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction decreed against the contested defendants including instant plaintiff appellant, then natural consequence is that the suit for sale permission for same suit plot is not maintainable when plaintiff himself especially in the plaint and evidences admitted that he is out of possession. 

 114. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned advocate for the appellant submits that the trial judge erred in law in adopting the evidence of PW 1 as a evidence of DW 1 in the respective cases. He further submits that in violation of section 33 of Evidence Act such adoption is not sustainable in law. Therefore, according to him the impugned judgments are liable to be set aside. In support of his contentions he relied upon to the case of Allah Ditta vs State reported in 11 DLR (SC) 38, and the case of Ali Haider reported in 10 DLR (SC) 193. I have gone through the aforesaid decisions as referred by the learned advocate. I have respectful agreement with principles enunciated therein, but the facts leading to those cases are quite distinguishable to that of the present case. Therefore, I am unable to accept the submissions of the learned advocate for the appellant. It further appears from the record that the defendants by applications dated 30-6-09 prayed for adoption of their depositions given as PW 1 in title suit Nos. 176 of 2004 and 51 of 2004 respectively as deposition of D.W. in title suit No. 81 of 06 at their own risk. So it is the plaintiffs of TS NOrs. 51 of 2004 and 176 of 04 by whose instance the adoption has been made. It will not be out of place to mention here that when the plaintiffs themselves applied in Court for adoption of their deposition to later proceedings pending before the same Court in respect of same suit land. Appellants surely would not be allowed to raise such questions before the appellale. Court without raising any question in trial and taking any grounds in the memo of appeal. 

 "No body is entitled to take benefit of his own wrong. To claiin that since no document has been executed the claimant has no right is nothing but taking advantage one's own wrong" 

 116. Two appeals mentioned above have been preferred against the judgment and decree of dismissal. From the judgments of the trial Court it appears that both the title suit have been dismissed by the trial Court as respective plaintiffs have failed to proVe their case. In this respect I have respectful agreement with my learned brother as from his judgment it appears that he has discussed the plaint case and the evidences in support of the plaint case wherein both of plaintiffs of title suit No. 51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 have failed to prove their cases in such situation I am of the view that provision of section 33 of Evidence Act has no manner of application in the instant appeal, in other words, it cannot be said that the trial judge erred in law in dismissing the title suit No. 51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004. 

 117. Now, II discuss and consider appeal from original decree No. 346 of 2009 preferred by Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza claiming himself as alive original Allottee and appeal from original decree No. 358 of 2009 preferred by MA Hashem defendant No.1 against the judgment and decree dated 06-8-2009 passed in title Suit No. 81 of 2006 filed by the Anowarul Hassan and others the heirs of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar decreed the suit. 

 118. In Title Suit No. 81 of 2006 the heirs of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza who were defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(e) in title suit No. 51 of 2004 filed the instant suit on the following prayers 

 121. At the time of trial plaintiffs led the evidences to prove their case and they examined as many as 5 PWs PW 1 Nasiruddin Khan, PW 2 Shamima Zaman, PW 3 Shahin Rahman, PW 4 Md. Abdul Quiyum and PW 5 Md. Arifur Rahman. Plaintiff to prove the case produced some documents in the Court and marked as exhibits, exhibit 1 authorisation letter of Eastern Housing, exhibit 2 dated 11-2-2004 power of attorney, exhibit 3 series are power of Attorneys dated 24-2-2004 and 01-3-2004, Exhibit-4 series are Matriculation certificate, Intermediate certificate, Engineer Part-I and part II certificate original copy for the year 1946, 1948, 1950 respectively, Exhibit-5 domicile certificate original copy dated 17-1-1952, Exhibit-6 deed Nos. 9847 and 6 (Ka) deed Nos. 9849 dated 28-9-1957 certified copy compared with original copy, Exhibit-7 deed No.31901 dated 17-8-1979 certified copy compared with original, Exhibit-8 approved residential plan of 157 Bara Moghbazar, Exhibit-9 voter list ID card No. 44100, 16540310234 dated 08-8-1999 and 9 (Ka) passport M-0510358 dated 03-12-96 in original of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, Exhibit-10 series higher training certificates of Canada Government, original letter of promotion Exhibit-11 series original certificates as Assistant Engineer and letter of promotion, Exhibit-12 series letter of allotment in original of suit plot and installment receipt in original, Exhibit-13 series 5 original installment deposit receipt of the National Bank of Pakistan showing deposit money to DIT paid by the Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, Exhibit-14 possession hand over letter dated 07-4-1962 by DIT to Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza, Exhibit-15 lease deed in original copy dated 01-8-1962 in favour of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza father of the plaintiffs and 15 (Ka) and 15 (Kha) are the signature of attesting witnesses. Exhibit-16 original copy of approved plan for the suit plot, exhibit 16 (Ka) is the permission of DIT. Exhibit-17 is the sanction letter of Housing Building Finance Corporation, exhibit 17 (ka) mortgage deed being No. 9022 dated 17-5-1967, Exhibit-18 series 10 copies deed of agreement for lease and rent agreement in respect of suit house, Exhibit-19 series Gas bill book, WASA demand notice, the taxes receipts of city corporation, exhibit 20 series are the assessment form, Tax and rent receipts, Exhibit-21 series copies of rent receipts, certified copy of RS record Exhibit-22, Exhibit-23 and 23 (Ka) are the Memorandum & Articles of Association, Exhibit-24 series are yearly report of Uttara Bank, Application receipt copy of Rajuk for approval of Rajuk for converting the suit plot residential to commercial plot is exhibit 25, the approval letter of RAJUK converting residential to commercial plot Exhibit-26, Exhibit-27 is the certified copy of power of attorney being No. 15902 dated 21-12-03 with photo executated by Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza in his life time in favour of Eastern Housing, exhibit 28 is the original received copy of RAJUK by which original power of attorney has been deposited to Rajuk office, Exhibit-29 series are the commercially approved plan copies of RAJUK, Exhibit-30 series are the notices dated 18-11-03 published in the Daily Inquilab, Janakantha, and the Observer and the protest notices dated 30-12-03, exhibit 31 series are the protest notice by which MA Hashem denied the existence of father of the plaintiffs, Exhibit-31(Kha) dated 2-2-04 is the copy of death certificate, exhibit 32 is the death certificate, Exhibit-33 is the notice dated 05-2-2004, Exhibit-34 is the certified copy of succession certificate issued in succession case being No. 439 of 2004 by Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. Exhibit 35 is the Photostat certified copies of Judgment of CR No.358 of 2004 and C.R.4608 of 2004 Exhibit-36 is the certified copy of plaint of T.S. 176 of 2004. Exhibit-37 is the pay bill of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. Exhibit-38 is the Passport No. B-057985 dated 15-1-75. 

 122. PW 1 produced and proved all the above mentioned exhibits in the Court at the time of his deposition without any objection from the defence. Considering the above exhibits it transpires that plaintiff Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza is the lessee of Dhaka improvement Trust now RAJUK and he had been exercising his right title and interest over the suit property from the year 1962 till his death within the full knowledge of all others. From Exhibit-15, 15 (ka), (15 kha) it reveals that its have been compared with the original standard lease deed kept in the custody of RAJUK. Therefore, RAJUK authority recognised the Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as his lessee. From Exhibit-14 dated 7-4-1962 it appears that possession of the suit plot was handed over to the father of the plaintiff, Exhibit-12 series are the original allotment letter and original copies of receipts of installment paid to the DIT by the father of the plaintiffs. Exhibit-17 sanction letter and 17 (ka) dated 17-5-1967 is mortgage deed of the suit plot in favour of the House Building. Finance Corporation and obtained loan mortgaging the suit land. Exhibit-18, 19 and 20 series are the bill copies of Gas, light, other taxes to the city corporation and rent receipt. Considering the above materials on record it appears that the father of the plaintiff after getting lease of the suit property from the RAJUK he has been exercising his continuous and uninterrupted title and possession over the same which proved beyond any doubt, Exhibit-25 and 26 proved that earlier suit plot was residential plot, however, at the instance of the plaintiff's father it has been converted to the commercial plot and Exhibit-27 and 28 proved that after converting to commercial plot RAJUK accepted the legal transfer fees and Exhibit-29 is approved plan of the multi-storied commercial plan of Eastern Housing Limited and accepted the Eastern Housing as the attorney of plaintiff's father from which is manifest and RAJUK accepted the father of the plaintiffs Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as lessee of RAJUK, however not accepted other two Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza one came from Mirpur and another living Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza as impleaded in the instant suit as defendant No.1 and defendant No-3. In this connection it may not be out of place to mention here that other two Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza claiming the suit property admittedly without possession and both of them made agreement for sale of the suit property not as admitted lessee of Rajuk because their papers and documents filed in title suit No.51 of 2004 and 176 of 2004 never produced before Rajuk and claimed that they are the allottee of RAJUK. 

 124. PW 2 Shamima Zaman in her deposition stated that engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza was her father. He died on 02-2-2004 in Central Hospital, Dhaka. Her father was a resident of 157 Bara Moghbazar. Her father died leaving 3 (three) sons and 2 (Two) daughters. Her father was executive engineer of C&B department later he joined as director of BDC of Islam Group. He also was a director of Uttara Bank. Her father never lived in section 6 House No. 31, Road No. 2 of Mirpur. Her father made an agreement and executed power of attorney in favour of Eastern Housing Limited. After the death of her father all the sisters and brothers of her including herself made 3 power of attorney in favour of Eastern Housing. Her father never made any contract with MA Hashem or MH Bhulu by executing any deed of agreement, 2 deeds of agreement submitted by the defendants which are false and fabricated. Thus against false and fabri-cated bainapatra they have filed the instant suit for cancellation the same. Defendants created false and forged bainapatra following the deeds of her father. Defendants also created forged signature of her father. There are no existence of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur. They contested in the title suit No. 51 of 2004 as defendant Nos. 1 (a) - 1(e) as the heirs of Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar not as heirs of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Mirpur, the evidence given in this suit may be adopted as the deposition of defendant nos. 1(a)-1(e) in title suit No. 51 of 2004. In cross examination he stated as per her deposition. In the cross examination the defence could not discover any contradictory statement nor made her evidences Shaky one. 

 126. PW 4 Md. Abdul Quiyum is a civil engineer of BUET. His father late Abdul Mannan was the friend of the plaintiff's father Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and both of them were the engineer of C&B they had been serving in the C&B department as engineer, later, his father transferred in DIT on deputation as executive engineer. His father was working as executive engineer in DIT while father of the plaintiffs got allotment of the suit plot. There was good relationship in between both of the family. There was communication between 2 family. There is a signature of his father in Exhibit-15 original lease deed dated 1-8-1962 made in between Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and the than DIT. He identified the signature of his father as exhibit 15 (ka) He further stated that in Exhibit-2 of title. suit No. 51 of 04 there is no signature of his father in the witness column, the Exhibit-2 has been created by forgery giving signature of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza of Bara Moghbazar. He also confirmed that he knows the signature of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza and signature in Exhibit-6 the alleged bainapatra of MA Hashem filed in title suit No. 51 of 2004 is not the signature of Executive Engineer Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza who is the friend of his father. 

 127. PW 5 Dr. Md. Arifur Rahman is the principle of National Medical College, Dhaka. He stated that on 3-7-77 he married the 2nd daughter Shahin Rahman of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. So he knows all the sons and daughters of Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza after their marriage they have been residing at 157 Bara Moghbazar with Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza. He died on 2-2-04 in Central Hospital, Dhaka. Before his death Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza came to know that one MA Hashem created forged bainapatra regarding his plot being No. 113 of Gulshan Avenue for which published a notice in the daily news papers stating that he did not make any contract agreement to anybody except Eastern Housing Limited. He further stated that late Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza never lived in outside of 157 Bara Moghbazar. His father in law never made any bainapatra with Mr. MA Hashem and with defendant No. 3 of this suit in other word with the plaintiff of title suit No. 176 of 2004. Bainapatra has been created by MA Hashem and the plaintiff of title Suit No. 176 of 2004 living Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza both the agreement are forged and executant of the bainapatra are the fake Shamsul Kabir Humayun Reza not his father-in-law who was a civil engineer. His father-in-law at first joined in the C&B department in the year 1952 as Assistant Engineer and later on in the year 1960 he was promoted to the post of Executive Engineer. In 1964 he joined in BDC as director of Islam Group and thereafter in the year 1966 he became a share director of Uttara Bank and till his death he was the director of Uttara Bank. In cross examination he denied the suggestion of the defence and specifically and categorically stated the facts as per his deposition. Defence has failed to discover any contradiction to his deposition by cross examination. 

 128. From discussions made above it is manifest that plaintiffs of title suit No. 81 of 2006 proved his own case.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 28 of 2009
parties:
Md. Mozaffer Rahman and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. The facts involved in the case, in short, are that the land recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 2 originally belonged to Penendu Narayan Roy Dev Barmon and his name has been recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 2 of the suit mouza; that the ex-landlord has given settlement of the suit land in favour of one Darkanath Dev and others but for arrears of rents ex-landlord has taken back the land in his khas possession from the aforesaid tenants. On 27.11.1951 B.S. the predecessor of the plaintiff namely Kalimuddin Mondal took pattan of the suit land as described in schedule 'Ka'. of the plaint from the aforesaid ex-landlord; that since the date of pattan the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs has been possessing the suit land measuring .24 acres of land with another .04 acres of land from another non suited plot but adjoining to the suit plot; that after the abolishment of zamindary system the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs became direct tenant of the Government and the Government recognized him as tenant of the suit land by realizing rents from him that during the period of M. R. R. operation the suit land recorded in the name of predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff's in M. R. R. Khatian No. 14 that thereafter, Kalimuddin died leaving behind the plain-tiffs as his legal heirs and since then the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land for more than 12(twelve) years; that in the recent revisional record of right, the suit land has been recorded in R. S. Khatian No. 1327; that the plaintiffs went to local Tahsil office for paying rents of the suit plot No. 698 but the Talisil office refused to take rents from them because plot No. 698 was not recorded in M. R. R. Khatian 14 that thereafter, the plaintiffs went to defendant No. 2, for correction of the record of right but he advised them to take shelter in the Civil Court; that on refusal to accept rents from the plaintiffs by the office of the defendant No. 2 the right, title of the plaintiffs over the suit land has been clouded, hence the suit. 

 4. Mr. Md. Mozammel Haque, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners submitted that the certified copies of the registered pattan dated 23.04.1945 which is the basic document of title of the plain-tiff for the suit land was filed in the Court of Appeal below by which the disputed land was given pattan to the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff by the orginal owner nor the supplementary affidavit filed at the time of hearing of the aforesaid civil revision, containing the certified copy of the aforesaid registered deed dated 23.04.1945 being the title. deed of the plaintiff was considered by the High Court Division; that after execution of the registered patta on 23.04.1945 by the original owner, whose title in the suit land became extinguished since the date of execution on 23.04.1945, title of the plain-tiff on the suit land had accrued on the aforesaid dated; that even if the original owner subsequently after 23.04.1945 had migrated to India which the defendant Government totally failed to prove and the evidence on record does not support the contention by the defendant that the suit land had vested in the Government so no question of passing of title to the Government does not arise at all, as title of the original owner had been extinguished, long ago on 23.04.1945 and passed to the plaintiff in the aforesaid registered pattan, executed and registered on 23.04.1945 by the original owner; that non-consideration of the aforesaid fact more particularly when oral evidence of a competent per-sons serves as secondary evidence under Section 63(4) of the Evidence Act of the certified copy of the aforesaid registered patta dated 23.04.1945 as well as of the supplementary affidavit filed in the Civil Revision. The learned Advocate further submitted that the Court of Appeal below most illegally and whimsically did not take into consideration the certified- copy of the registered patta dated 23.04.1945 nor take those into evidence in exercise of power under Section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thus, by an erroneous view agreeing with the finding of the Court of Appeal below committed an error of law in holding that the plaintiff had miserably failed 'to establish its right and title in the suit land which is contrary to the evidence. 

 5. It appears that the trial Court as well as the Court of Appeal below on consideration of the evidence, both oral and documentary found that the plaintiffs could not prove their right and title in the suit land. It appears that in the instant case, the plaintiffs claimed their predecessor-in-interest became tenant of the suit land by way of pattan as well as oral gift but at the trial the plaintiff could not prove neither the story of pattan nor the oral gift by adducing any reliable or documentary evidence. It also appears that the plaintiffs had no title to the suit land and the story of pattan as well as oral gift is false. Accordingly, both the Courts below rightly and correctly arrived at a finding that the plaintiffs failed to establish their right and title in the suit land.

parties:
Younusco K Textiles Ltd. ----- Defendant-Appellant
vs. 
Jamuna Knitting and Dyeing Ltd & others ----- Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Appeal No. 234 of 2004 is from judgment and decree dated 18-4-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur. 

 3. Similarly, Appeal No. 235 of 2004 arose out of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 of the aforesaid Court and both the suits were heard analogously by the Court below and by common judgment dated 18-4-2004 both suits were disposed of by the impugned judgment. The trial Court by the impugned judgment decreed both the suits and allowed the prayer for pre-emption made by the plaintiffs in respect of 'A' Schedule property of the respective suits as Shafi-i-Jar under the Muslim Law and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment the defendant has preferred these appeals before this Court. 

 5. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiffs have title to and possession in the 'B' Schedule property by purchase and plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 have title to and possession in 2.58 acres of land i.e. the 'B' Schedule land, which are contiguous to the suit land i.e. 'A' Schedule land in the southern side. The further case is that the plaintiffs have seen construction of wall in 'A' Schedule land in the later part of 1995 by the defendant No. 2 Company as owner. The positive case of the plaintiffs is that on 9-3-1997 the plaintiff No. 2 along with 2 other persons, namely, Messrs Ershad Hossain and Md Ismail Meah were passing through 'A' Schedule land when plaintiff No. 2 found one Abu Bakar Siddique living in a newly constructed CI sheet but and on his query as to who raised the but and how he was living there Abu Bakar Siddique disclosed that the defendant No. 2 Company had sold the 'A' Schedule property to defendant No. 1 Company and defendant No. 1 had raised the but for him as he is the caretaker of defendant No. 1 and upon hearing this the plaintiff No. 2 for self and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 at once made Talab-i-Muwsibat and asserted their purported right to pre-empt the said land in presence of the said two persons and thereafter, he sent a man to make a query to the local registration office who obtained certified copy of the kabalas in question on 18-3-1997 when he definitely came to learn about the aforesaid transfer and made Talab-i-Ishhad in presence of witnesses telling that Talab-i-Muwsibat had already been made on 9-3-1997. This time Messrs Ershad Hossain and Aman Ali and some other employees of Plaintiff No. 1's company went upon the land of 'A' Schedule. The purchaser is stranger whereas the plaintiffs are neighbors and, as such, they have instituted the suit under the Muslim Law to pre-empt the 'A' Schedule land after due compliance with the formalities as are required under the Muslim Law. 

 8. Mr Tabarak Hussain thereafter made his submission on the merits of the appeal. His first submission is that even if it is found by this court that Muslim Law of pre-emption is a valid law then also the instant suits are not maintainable under the Muslim Law because the plaintiffs are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for, inasmuch as on two. grounds the plaintiffs have instituted the suits, namely, as Shafi-i-Khalid and Shafi-i-Jar and from the impugned judgment it is found that the trial Court found that the plaintiffs were not entitled to get an order of pre-emption as Shafi-i-Khalid and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-respondents as Shafi-i-Jar and the plaintiffs have not preferred any cross-appeal against that finding of the trial Court. Mr Hussain now submits that the suit land cannot be the subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law and the plaintiffs cannot invoke the law as Shafi-i-jar, inasmuch as the subject matter is not 'Agar' or land nor the suit land is 'Ruba' or mansion or 'hait' or garden i.e. he contends that a person can invoke the Muslim Law of pre-emption as a Shafi-i-Jar only in respect of a homestead or mansion, garden or small piece of land and in the instant case admittedly, the 'A' Schedule land is not a homestead nor it is garden adjoining to any homestead nor it is a small piece of land, inasmuch as the plaintiffs have instituted the suits for pre-empting 8.69 acres of land. In this connection, he relied on Digest of Muslim Law by Bailee, Tybee’s Muslim Law, section 539 and 12 DLR 93. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits that it is apparent from the materials and evidence on record that the suit lands have been purchased by the appellant company in order to set up industry and before that the vendor company also bought the land with an intention to set up industry and therefore, the Muslim Law of pre-emption has no manner of application to commercial plots and in decreeing the suit the trial Court lost sight of this important question of law that right of pre-emption cannot be enforced in case of commercial plots. For this proposition, Mr Hussain relies on the case reported in PLD 1990 (Karachi) 387. Mr Hussain made another plank of attack on the impugned judgment by submitting that in decreeing the suits, the trial Court has also committed another illegality in not giving any finding as to the necessity of the suit land by the plaintiffs. In elaborating his submission the learned Advocate further submits that the case of the plaintiffs is that they require the lands for their own purpose but what is the purpose has neither been explained in the plaint nor in the evidence. They simply made a vague statement that the land is required for them. To fortify his submission he contends that one of the stringent principles of law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law is that one cannot resort to pre-emption for his enrichment at the cost of the buyer. Therefore, the plaintiffs were under the legal obligation to explain the necessity of acquiring the 'A' Schedule land by them. But they have miserably failed to discharge their onus on that point. In support of this contention the learned Advocate relied on the decision reported in PLD 1991 (Lahore) 217. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits, with much emphasis, that the plaintiffs filed the suits for pre-emption as contiguous land owners and thus, they are to prove their ownership of the contiguous land and also required to prove that the legal formalities for the purpose of the Talabs, namely Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad, have been performed at the earliest opportune moment but the plaintiffs have failed to show or establish their ownership or 'Milk' to the 'B' Schedule land by producing cogent evidence both oral and documentary and until and unless the plaintiffs can establish their ownership to the 'B' Schedule land, the plaintiffs will have no locus standi to maintain the suit. In the instant case, the plaintiffs have examined 3 witnesses including plaintiff No. 2 in support of their case but surprisingly, the plaintiffs, for reasons best known to them, did not examine any impartial witness and thus have miserably failed to prove that they are the owners of the 'B' Schedule land and to establish the ownership no document of title has been produced or admitted into evidence by the plaintiffs before the trial Court to establish their title to 'B' Schedule land and it was incumbent upon the plaintiffs to prove their ownership to the 'B' Schedule land in view of the fact that it has been specifically stated by the defendants in their written statement that the plaintiffs are not the owner of contiguous 'B' Schedule land. Mr Tabarak Hussain further submits that the settled proposition of law is that only the owners of the contiguous land can maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim Law as Shafi-i-jar but, in the instant suits, the plaintiffs miserably failed to prove their title to the contiguous land and, in that view of the matter, mere possession of the 'B' Schedule land will not give them any ladder to pre-empt the land. In support of his contention, he relies on the decisions reported in 12 DLR 93 and 1983 CLC 1883. 

 9. Mr Tabarak Hussain then comes up with another formidable submission and referring to the evidence on record, he submitted that the plaintiff No. 2 in his evidence stated that he does not know what are the requirements of Shafi-i-jar or Shafi-i-Khalid and what formalities are required to perform Talab-i-Muwsibat or Talab-i-Ishhad and this frank and open admission of the plaintiff No. 2 has demolished the entire case of the plaintiffs, inasmuch as a person who does not know what formalities are required to perform for valid performance of Talabs, it is impossible on his part to perform the same. This piece of evidence belies the story of performance of the said Talabs by the plaintiff’s No. 2. In elaborating his submission Mr Hussain submitted that the plaintiff No. 2 as PW 1 said that he performed Talab-i-Muwsibat by saying that he would have bought the 'A' Schedule land and he will exercise right of pre-emption but none of the PWs namely, PWs 2 and 3, supported him in their deposition. Therefore, the plaintiffs failed to prove the performance of the Talabs made by him as claimed in his evidence. Mr Tabarak Hussain further contends that to get a decree for pre-emption under the Muslim Law there must be stringent compliance with the formalities and performance of the formalities must be clearly proved which is absent in the present suits. Mr Tabarak Hussain further submits that the evidence of the PWs shows that the PW 1 did not utter any word to exercise the right of pre-emption whereas law requires that the pre-emptor must express his intention of exercising the right of pre-emption in some way. To further strengthen his submission Mr Tabarak Hussain submits that there is nothing at all on record to show that the formalities of Talabs were performed by the plaintiff No. 1 Company. In this connection, he relies on the decision reported in 49 CWN 761. Mr Tabarak Hussain to fortify his submission submits that the plaintiff No. 1 claimed in the plaint that he performed Talab-i-Muwsibat in the suit land but in evidence he stated that he performed the same standing on the land near the suit lands. Thus, the testimony of PW 1 itself established that Talab-i-Muwsibat was not performed in the suit land. Mr Tabarak Hussain drawing our attention to the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 submitted that they do not support the plaintiffs on this point about the Talab-i-Muwsibat and failure on the part of the plaintiffs to prove the Talab-i-Muwsibat disentitled the plaintiffs to get any relief in the suits. Mr Hussain then submits that the trial Court on misreading and non-consideration of material portion of evidence erroneously held that Talab-i-Muwsibat was properly performed by the plaintiffs for the suit land and thereby the instant appeals are liable to be allowed in the light of the principle of law as laid down in 10 ILR Calcutta 383. Mr Hussain further submitted that the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside yet on another ground i.e. legal pro-position of law is that under the Muslim Law the pre-emptor is required to make Talab-i-Ishhad with the least delay but in the instant case according to the plaint, they came to know about the sale of the suit property on 9-3-1997 and after obtaining certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 they made Talab-i-Ishad on 19-3-1997. In this connection he further contends that in making the alleged Talab-i-Ishhad the plaintiffs have failed to comply with the provisions of law because under the Muslim Law pre-emptor is required to make Talab-i-Ishhad either in the presence of the seller or the purchaser or on the subject matter referring to the earlier demand and invoking two witnesses. In this case the admitted position is that the Talab-i-Ishhad was not made either in presence of the seller or the purchaser nor on the suit land. From the evidence on record it appears that the story of making Talab-i-Ishhad by the plaintiff No. 2 on the suit land has not been proved and this aspect of the case was not considered by the trial Court, Mr Hussain contends. In this connection, Mr Tabarak Hussain relies on the decision reported in ILR 17 Calcutta 544, 1991 CLC Karachi 209, 19 DLR 759 and ILR 28 Allahabad 24. Mr Tabarak Hussain referring to the evidence of PW 1 submitted that he himself admitted in his evidence that there is boundary wall on all sides of the suit land and there is only one gate in the eastern side leading to Kashimpur Road and the admitted position is that the plaintiffs' land and the suit lands are demarcated by boundary wall of 7" 6" height all around it. Therefore, there is no contiguity in between the plaintiffs land and the suit land and on that score also the suits were liable to be dismissed. Mr Tabarak Hussain, drawing our attention to the evidences adduced by the PWs, submitted that there are material discrepancies in the evidence of the PWs and on scrutiny it is found that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their case in accordance with the requirement of the Muslim Law. Mr Hussain seriously criticized the finding of the trial Court that the suits are not barred by limitation and in arriving at such a finding the trial Court relied on the evidence of PW 1 who stated that on 9-3-1997 he came to know about the sale of 'A' Schedule land to the defendant No. 1 and then after obtaining certified copy of the sale deeds he made the Talab-i-Ishhad and the instant suits were filed within the period of limitation of one year as contemplated by Article 10 of the Limitation Act. But in affirming at such a finding the trial Court is guilty of non-consideration of the evidence adduced by the DWs coupled with Exhibits A, C and Cl and therefore, erroneously arrived at such a finding and the said finding of the trial Court is contrary to law, inasmuch as it is now well settled within our jurisdiction that under the Muslim Law sale is complete when the vendor on receipt of consideration money inducts the buyer into the possession of land and in the instant case Exhibit 'C' series were presented for registration on 7-3-1996 and from the Exhibit 'C' series it is clear that on receipt of full consideration money the possession of the vendee was confirmed as they were already in possession of the suit property earlier pursuant to the agreement of sale vide Exhibit 'A' and the finding of the trial Court on this point is not sustainable in law, inasmuch as it has been decided by both the Divisions of this Court in the cases reported in 31 DLR 249 and 33 DLR (AD) 359 that in case of pre-emption suit filed under Muslim Law the sale of property shall not be governed by the provisions of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and, for that matter, the provisions of sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act have no manner of application and in order to complete a sale of any property to enable a person to claim pre-emption under Muslim Law, one shall not wait till the completion of all formalities as contemplated under section 61 of the Registration Act and the cause of action arises as soon as the sale is complete under the Muslim Law independent of any written instrument, and here the trial Court fell into an error in holding that the instant suits were not barred by limitation and, in this connection, Mr Hussain has relied on the case reported in 3 DLR 225. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits that Appeal No. 235 of 2004 arose out of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 but in the course of evidence PW 1 did not utter a single word in respect of the performance of Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad in respect of the land of this suit. He further submitted that the land of Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 and the title suit No. 101 of 1997 are not one and same and therefore, there is no contiguity of the land of 'B' Schedule with the suit land of suit No. 101 of 1997 and this fact becomes evident from the map of the Advocate Commissioner filed in the suit. It is also contended by Mr Tabarak Hussain that right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is not available to the plaintiffs, inasmuch as the suit lands are neither houses nor small plot of land and therefore, the suits were misconceived and not tenable in law and in decreeing the suit this aspect of law was overlooked by the trial Court and, as such, the impugned judgments are liable to be set aside. 

 11. Mr Enayet Hossain Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondents in both the appeals, submits that the trial Court taking a correct view of law rightly decreed the suits, inasmuch as the suits are very much maintainable in the present form and manner. In elaborating his submission, he draws our attention to section 231 of the Muslim Law by Mollah and submits that in that section it has been specified what classes of persons can initiate and maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim Law and the expression 'person' includes both natural and jural person. Therefore, the suits instituted by the plaintiffs cannot fail on the ground that the plaintiff No. 1 in both the suits is a company because persons contemplated in that section includes a legal entity and no bar has been imposed on a company under the Muslim Law to file a suit for pre-emption if it fulfils other requirements as laid down in the Muslim Law. The learned Advocate then submits that the trial Court on the basis of the averments of the respective parties framed 3 issues and the appellants are not entitled to make any submission beyond the issues framed by the trial Court and therefore, the appellant must confine themselves in assailing the legality or otherwise of the impugned judgment on the issues that were framed by the trial Court and cannot travel beyond the issues framed by the trial Court for disposal of the instant suits and since the trial Court has found Issue No. 1 in favour of the plaintiffs, it does not lie in the mouth of the appellants to come and say that the suits are not maintainable under the Muslim Law and that the plaintiff No. 1 had no locus standi to institute such a suit. To fortify his argument he relied on the provisions of Order XIV, rule 1 and submitted that a litigant cannot be given the liberty to travel beyond the issues, mores, when the defendants were satisfied with the issues framed by the trial Court. The learned Advocate very empathically submitted that the finding of the trial Court that the suit is not barred by limitation is based on evidence on record, inasmuch as the documents produced by the defendants show that the finding is backed by sufficient materials on record and in elaborating his submission on this point he refers to Clause No. 3 of the agreement dated 16-8-1995 executed by the defendant No. 2 in favour of the defendant No. 1 appellant and it has been clearly stipulated that with the execution of the said agreement the vendee will construct the boundary wall on all sides of the property but the possession will remain with the vendor legally, validly and physically and further that the purchaser shall not claim possession of the property before registration of the sale deed or deeds in favour of the purchaser and relying on the aforesaid clause of Exhibit 'A', submitted that this clearly states the intention of the parties that the title to the property in question will be passed to the buyer when the registration is completed under the Registration Act and the registration was completed on 9-3-1997. Therefore, the trial Court taking a correct view of law rightly held that the suits were instituted within the period of limitation as laid down in Article 10 of the Limitation Act, 1908. He further submitted that in view of the specific stipulation as laid down in Exhibit 'A' mere presentation of the documents for registration on 7-3-1996, did not complete the sale on that date and provision as laid down in Muslim Law will not be applicable in computing the period of limitation. Mr Khan then submits that much emphasis has been given by the appellants that the suit lands are not agricultural land they are commercial lands and thus the suits as framed are misconceived ones and not tenable in law but he submits that it does not reflect the correct state of affairs as contemplated by Muslim Law. Under the Muslim Law a person can initiate a proceeding to exercise the right of pre-emption in respect of an immovable property of any description and it is immaterial whether it is homestead or agricultural or commercial plot and that cannot be a ground for setting aside the impugned judgment. 

 13. Mr Khan then turns his attention on the merit of the appeal and submits that the trial Court on consideration of the pleadings, the evidence adduced by the parties and taking into consideration the materials on record rightly found that the plaintiffs have complied with the formalities of Talab-i-Muw-sibat and Talab-i-Ishhad within the meaning of the Muslim Law. in elaborating his argument on this point, he submits that the plaintiff No. 2 has performed those formalities for and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 and on his behalf though at the time of deposition he stated that he made the Talabs for pre-empting the properties under the Muslim Law and there is no discrepancy in the evidence of PWs. The learned Advocate for the respondent submits that there is no specific form for performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat though certain formalities have been laid down for the performance of Talab-i-Ishhad and from the deposition of PW 1 it becomes clear that the specific intention for pre-empting the suit land by the plaintiffs have been expressed on 9--1997 by performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat on the suit land. Mr Khan further submitted that it does not lie in the mouth of the appellant to say that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their ownership in the 'B' Schedule land, inasmuch as the DWs in one voice admitted in their evidence that to the contiguous south of the suit land, the land of the plaintiffs are situated. Mr Khan submitted that there is sufficient oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs stating that they are the purchaser of 'B' Schedule land and the certified copies of the deeds in question have been exhibited by the plaintiffs before the trial Court and the original title deeds could not be produced as they are lying with the Bank. In elaborating his submission he further submits that besides the PWs the DWs also admitted that the plaintiffs are the owner of the 'B' Schedule land and the legal position is that things admitted need not be proved. There-fore, even in the absence of any evidence the trial Court is justified in arriving at a finding that the plaintiffs are the real owner of the 'B' Schedule land and thereby the first pre-requisite for filing of the suit for pre-emption by the plaintiffs have been fulfilled. Mr Khan further submitted that Mr Tabarak Hussain forcefully argued that the suit lands are not agricultural land and are commercial plots, but this submission is contrary to material and evidence on record. Exhibits 5(Kha) and 3 (Gha) i.e. Khatian and rent receipt, as well as the title deeds of the defendant No. 1 show that the suit land is agricultural land and the 'B' Schedule land is Chala land and Chala land is also agricultural land within the meaning of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951. Therefore, it cannot be said that the lands in question are commercial plots and therefore, cannot be a subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. Mr Khan further submitted that to prove the ownership of the 'B' Schedule land the plaintiffs produced and exhibited current rent receipts which have been admitted without any objection and it is now well settled that khatian and rent receipts are documents of possession and collateral documents of title as has been laid down in 35 DLR (AD) 216. Mr Khan further submitted that it has been contended by the appellants that the plaintiffs did not make the Talab-i-Ishhad promptly but there is no basis for that as admitted facts show that the plaintiffs first came to know about the sale in question on 9-3-1997 and on the next date sent their man to the local Registry Office and obtained the certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 when the plaintiffs acquired a definite know-ledge as to the sale of the suit lands by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 to the defendant No. 1 and then on 19-3-1997 made Talab-i-Ishhad. Mr Enayet Hossain Khan in the course of argument also submitted that in a suit for pre-emption the plaintiffs need not establish their title, inasmuch as the title of the plaintiffs is not in issue and it has been categorically stated by the plaintiffs in their plaint that they are owner by purchase of the 'B' Schedule land which has not been denied by the defendants in their written statement. Therefore, it must be presumed that the defendants have admitted the aforesaid statement of the plaintiffs and now they cannot resale from that and take a different stand giving a go-by to the earlier stand. Mr Khan also submitted that the trial Court has rightly taken the view that the boundary wall erected in between the 'A' and 'B' Schedule lands cannot stand in the way of the plaintiffs to get an order of pre-emption in their favour inasmuch as the 'B' Schedule land is contiguous to 'A' Schedule land. 

 Who may claim pre-emption. The following three classes of persons and no others, are entitled to claim pre-emption, namely: 

 owners of adjoining immovable property (z) (shafi-i-jar), but not their tenants (a), nor persons in possession of such property without any lawful title (b) (Baillie, 481). 

 20. In the light of our aforesaid observation, let us now see if the privilege conferred upon a Muslim citizen to invoke the law of pre-emption, as a Shafi-i-Jar imposes any unreasonable restriction upon a citizen either in the matter of acquiring a property or holding a property and/or in the matter for transfer of property. We have already indicated that Muslim law of pre-emption applies to both town and village property and we have to judge the reasonableness of the law in the context of the fundamental rights which have been conferred upon the citizens by the Constitution on the people of this country and which were not there when the Courts in the Sub-continent have considered the reasonableness of the law. If there were no law of pre-emption a vendor would be entitled to sell his property to anybody at a reasonable price that could be settled between him and the purchaser. This right to transfer property freely is clearly restricted by the law of pre-emption which in many cases results in depression of the price which the vendor could otherwise be able to get for his property. Similarly, it also imposes a restriction on a citizen to acquire a property. Suppose, if a property is bought by a landless people and the contiguous land-holder as a Shafi-i-Jar pre-empts the sale and substitutes himself for the purchaser, in such a situation the purchaser is in a helpless situation. He has money to buy property but he cannot acquire it because of the sword of Shafi-i-Jar which hangs over his shoulder. It also adversely affects the vendor in that he cannot get the proper price from a prospective buyer as the prospective buyer will be always under the threat of losing his newly acquired property through an action of pre-emption. It, therefore, appears to us that the privilege available to a Muslim citizen as a Shafi-i-Jar adversely affects the interest of both the vendor and the vendee and in a country where there is explosion of population and tremendous pressure on land the attempt to keep the land in the hands of the contiguous land holder cannot be justified. Moreover, this right of contiguous land owner also offends the rule against perpetuity as the lands are not allowed to change hands freely. As a result the possibility of development of land and improvement of quality in the life of the community suffers. In the context of present- day reality and the globalization of the world the restriction imposed on transfer of property and/or acquiring property by the law of pre-emption, such as Shafi-i-Jar, cannot be encouraged as such a restriction impedes national interest. 

 23. Now it requires us to advert to the question of maintainability of the suits under the Muslim Law. The admitted position is that in the instant case both the vendor and one of the vendees are companies incorporated under the Companies Act. A company is, no doubt, a rural person having its own entity and can sue or be sued in its own name but it is not a natural person like a normal human being. Moreover, a company exists independently of its shareholders and shareholders are not the owner of the company. A company being a juridical person is incapable of professing any faith. The admitted position is that Muslim Law is the personal law of the Musalmans. The legal position is that personal law of vendor governs a transaction of sale of immovable property and not that of vendee for the purpose of determining the right of Suffa i.e. pre-emption. A company being an artificial person cannot have any faith in any religion and therefore when the vendor of an immovable property is a company the Muslim Law cannot have any manner of application to that transaction. Two legal propositions have been laid down by the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case reported in ILR 1 ALL. (FB) 564. The first one is that even if one of the preemptors is Muslim nevertheless the pre-emption will be governed by the personal law of the vendor and the second one is that where the vendor is a Hindu a suit to enforce the right of pre-emption founded on Muslim Law is not sustainable. In the instant case, vendor is a company so also is one of the vendees i.e. plaintiff No. 1 is a company and they are incapable of having any faith in any religion. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case there is no scope to invoke the provisions of Suffa under the Muslim Law. The suits are misconceived and not maintainable in their present forms and manner. In this connection it may be mentioned that Mr Khan half heartedly urged before us that in section 231 of Muslim Law it is stated that three classes of persons are entitled to claim pre-emption and since a company is a legal person it can maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim law. This submission is absolutely devoid of any substance. What is Muslim law? It is the personal law of a Musalman and who is a Musalman? A natural person who professes the Islamic Faith, that is, acknowledges that there is but one Allah and that Mohammad (SM) is his Prophet. A person can be Musalman either by birth or by conversion. Thus only a natural person can become a Musalman and profess the faith of Islam. A juridical person is incapable of following any religion. The courts today apply Muslim Law to the Musalmans only and this power is derived from and regulated partly by Statutes of Imperial Parliament read with Article 152 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and also by our own legislation and the rules of Muslim Law of pre-emption are applied to Muslims as a matter of justice, equity and good conscience. It must also be remembered that right of pre-emption is not a purely Islamic Institution. It emanates partly from Arab Customs and partly from local customs. It was created in a Shafi (pre-emptor) by Hadis of Holy Prophet (SM).Thus we find force and substance in this submission of Mr Hussain and hold that the suits as framed are not maintainable under the Muslim Law. It is true plaintiff No. 2 is a natural person but the suits as framed cannot be maintained by him solely as there is no averments in the plaint nor in evidence to show contiguity of his land with the suit land. 

 25. These appeals were heard at length and both the parties argued extensively both on point of law and facts. Therefore, we would also like to address all the issues that were raised by the parties. The trial Court found the suits not barred by limitation whereas it is contended by the appellants that the suits are barred by limitation. Mr Khan relying on clause 3 of the agreement, Exhibit 'A' submitted that it is clearly laid down in that clause that title of the vendor will remain with them until and unless the sale deed is registered and the sale deeds were entered in the volume on 5-3-1997 and Talab-i-Muwsibat was made on 9-3-1997 and after obtaining certified copy on 18-3-1997, Talab-i-Ishhad was made on the following day. Therefore, the suits as filed on 30-3-1997 are well within the period of limitation. As against that, Mr. Hussain's contention is that under the Muslim Law sale becomes complete on delivery of possession of immovable property on receipt of consideration. The sale deeds were presented for registration on 7-3-1996. Thus, if the sale in question is governed by the rules of Muslim Law sale was completed on 7-3-1996 as it appears from Exhibit 'C' series that both the deeds were presented for registration on 7-3-1996 and possession of the suit land was also handed over to the defendant-appellant long before the execution and presentation of the sale deeds for registration pursuant to agreement for sale vide Exhibit 'A'. 

 29. Let us, now, discuss about the merits of the appeals. The defendants have denied the ownership of the plaintiffs in the "B" Schedule land in paragraph No. 12 of the written statement as well as DW 1 has denied it in his evidence. As against that the plaintiffs made out a case in their plaint that they are the owners by purchase of the "B" Schedule land but at the time of adducing evidence except the word of PW 1 there is no other documentary evidence to show that they are the real owners of the "B" Schedule land. It is stated by PW 1 that the original title deeds are lying with the bank and a letter to that effect of the Bank was produced but they have not admitted in evidence the certified copy of the title deeds. Mr Tabarak Hussain empathically argued on this point submitting that it is pre-requisite for the plaintiffs to prove their ownership in the contiguous land. Even before this Court the plaintiff respondent did not file any application under Order XL, rule 31 of the Code to admit those documents as additional evidence. Moreover, there is no explanation why they have not exhibited the title deeds which are the most important documents for proving the title of the plaintiffs to 'B' Schedule land. To counter the arguments of Mr Hussain, Mr Khan appearing for the plaintiff-respondent tried to impress upon us that though title deeds have not been exhibited nevertheless khatians and rent receipts which are collateral documents of title have been produced and exhibited. Mr Khan relying on the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 submitted that record of rights and rent receipts are collateral documents of title and these are sufficient to establish the title of the plaintiff. As against that, Mr Hussain has submitted that in a pre-emption suit it is the sine qua non to establish the ownership of the plaintiff and by withholding the original documents without giving any explanation and production of Khatian and rent receipts are not sufficient to establish the title and in support of his contention he has relied on the decision reported in 12 DLR 93. In this connection it may further be mentioned that though they have produced some certified copies of the deeds but that only relates to 2.58 acres of land and regarding the rest of the land no title deed has been filed and ignoring this material aspect of the case, the trial Court arrived at a finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their owner-ship simply on the ground that even the DWs have admitted plaintiffs' ownership. This observation of the trial Court appears to be based on misreading of the evidence of DWs. It appears that DW 1 categorically denied the ownership of the plaintiffs and the other DWs admitted that the plaintiffs are in possession of the 'B' Schedule land. But they did not indicate the nature of possession as to whether they possess it as owners or otherwise. It is now well established that in a pre-emption suit the plaintiff must establish his exclusive ownership into the contiguous land as Shafi-i-Jar. Therefore, finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs are the owners of the 'B' Schedule land is erroneous and against weight of evidence. 

 43. Before we part with these appeals, we need to advert to the other appeal that is Appeal No. 235 of 2004. We have already noted that two suits were filed by the plaintiffs in respect of two different sale deeds and they were registered as Title Suit No. 100 of 2004 and 101 of 2004 respectively and both the suits were heard analogously by taking one set of evidence and by a common judgment both the suits were decreed. From the impugned judgment it appears that the trial Court disposed of both the suits on the basis of issues framed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997. From the record of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997, it appears that in that suit two more issues were framed. But at the time of writing out the judgment, the trial Court was confined to issues framed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 and did not at all care to give any finding about the other two issues framed in the later suit. In disposing Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 the trial Court did not deal with the said issues which demonstrate that the trial Court most negligently and without applying its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case in a mechanical way decreed the suit without properly addressing the relevant issues. 

 44. It has already been indicated that both the appeals are being disposed of by this Judgment and at the time of advancing argument Mr Khan however did not advance any argument in respect of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 that is Appeal No. 235 of 2004. It is admitted that the land of Appeal No. 235 of 2004 and the land of Appeal No. 234 of 2004 were purchased by two different kabalas, but the plaintiffs did not adduce any evidence whatsoever in respect of Talabs for the land of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 and this is a material omission and failure on the part of the plaintiff-respondents to prove that they had also exercised their right of pre-emption in respect of the land of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 and that they had performed the Talabs, the plaintiffs cannot get any relief in Appeal No. 235 of 1994 on this score alone. Mr Hussain urged this point emphatically for the second appeal, but in our opinion it is of no importance, inasmuch as we have already found on merits that the appeals are liable to be allowed as the trial Court judgment suffers from patent illegality and infirmity and is not sustainable in law. Thus, no doubt, the omission on the part of the plaintiffs to adduce evidence in respect of the suit land of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 is fatal and this is an additional ground but our finding given on all other points are common to both the appeals, therefore, in any view of the matter, the appeals are liable to be allowed. 

 45. In the result, both the appeals are allowed judgment and decree dated 184-2004 (decree signed on 18-8-2004) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 and Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 are set aside and both the suits are dismissed. The defendant-appellant No. 1 will get cost in both the suits against the plaintiffs.

caseno: Civil Petition For Leave To Appeal No. 304 of 1998
parties:
M/s. Sekander Jute Bailing Ltd. ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Sonali Bank and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Respondent-Bank as plaintiff obtained an ex-parte decree for Tk. 81,16,891.12 against the petitioner as recovery of loan in Title Suit No. 223 of 1990 from the 2nd Artha Rin Adalat, Khulna by judgment and decree dated 25.11.91. The petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 36 of 1993 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Khulna on 20.10.93 for setting aside the ex-parte decree on the ground of fraud and collusion. By an order dated 17.11.93 the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the plaint on an application by the defendant-respondent on the ground that the suit is not maintainable in view of the remedy available to the petitioner against the judgment passed by the Artha Rin Adalat under the Artha Rin Adalat Act itself. The plaintiff-petitioner filed the above Civil Revision unsuccessfully, as the High Court Division took the same view. 

 3. Mr. Abdul Baset Majumder, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that when the decree was passed in the original Title Suit in 1991 there was no provision for preferring an application under Order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aside an ex-parte decree. That provision was introduced in 1992 with prospective effect. This means that the legislature being aware of the predicament of the judgment-debtors made other remedies available to the judgment-debtor apart from the remedy of appeal to the High Court Division with a deposit of 50% of the decretal dues. Since the legislature has taken a liberal view of the difficulties of the judgment-debtor this Court may also take a similar view with regard to the plight of the judgment-debtor in respect of an ex-parte decree passed before 1992 and make a title suit maintainable in the absence of any remedy other than an appeal to the High Court Division with onerous obligations.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury
case_type_name: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal

parties:
Mohammad Shamsul Alam and others ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Md. Abdul Malek Tapadar and others ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
D.M. Ansaruddin Ahmed, J.: This Rule issued at the instance of plaintiffs Nos. 2 to 6 on an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the Judgment and decree passed on 24.9.1991 by the Subordinate Judge; Noakhali, in Title Appeal No. 245 of 1985 reversing those passed on 30.11.1985 by the Munsif , Chatkhil, decreeting Title Suit No. 30 of 1985 (Originally Title Suit No. 200 of 1079 of the Munsif 2nd court, Laximpur corresponding to Title Suit no 43 of 1983 of the Munsifs Court, Ramganj). 

 4. The defendant Md. Abdul Malek Tapadar contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaintiffs' allegations and contending inter alia that in pursuance of a talk with him the plaintiff received the entire amount of the consideration money, executed the kabala in his favour and got it registered and delivered possession of the properties in his favour and since then he is in possession thereof. It was further contended that the original kabla was stolen away along with other valuable articles when there was a theft in his house. 

 6. At the trial 4 witnesses were examined on either side including plaintiff No. 6 Akhtarul Alam and the contesting defendant. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the materials on record held that the impugned kabala was a forged and fraudulent document and he accordingly decreed the suit. Against the judgment and decree, the defendant preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 245 of 1985 which has been heard by the learned Subordinate Judge. The learned Judge has noticed the circumstances under which the plaintiff's prayer for examination of thumb impressions appearing in the Thumb Impression Register of the Registration office was rejected. He has also taken into consideration the fact that the plaintiff Chandra Narayan Shamadhikari who has been living in this country did not oath to deny the execution of the kabala and that D.W.2 Chowdhury Mia and D.W.3 Badsha Mia, both the attesting witnesses of the Kabala, deposed to the effect that the plaintiff Chandra Narayan Sharmadhikari executed the Kabala in their presence. Referring to the evidence given by P.W. 4 Abul Hosain Molla, Chairman of the local Union Parishad the learned Judge has held that the witness admitted the defendant's possession in the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge found that the kabala was executed by plaintiff Chandra Narayan Sharmadhikari and got it registered. He has, accordingly, allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and dismissed the suit. Against this appellate judgment and decree, the plaintiff's Nos. 2 to 6 have obtained the instant Rule. 

 8. On a perusal of the judgment rendered by the learned Subordinate Judge, it appears that he has taken due notice of the relevant facts and circumstances in arriving at his decision. In assailing the impugned kabala, the burden was squarely upon plaintiff Chandra Narayan Shamadhikari whose name appears therein as the executant, to take oath and say that it was not executed by him. The said plaintiff is alive and living in this country. The primary burden having not been discharged by the plaintiffs, there is no burden upon the defendant to prove that the document is genuine. In addition, the plaintiffs have failed to take necessary steps for getting examined by an expert the thumb impressions of the executant of the Kabala appearing in the Thumb Impression Register of the Registration Office. On the other hand, the defendant has examined both the attesting witnesses who have stated that it was the plaintiff Chandra Narayan Sharmadhikari who executed the document in their presence. There is also the evidence of the plaintiffs' own witness No. 4, who is the Chairman of the local Union Parishad, who has stated that he had seen the defendant possessing the suit land at a time prior to the kabalas obtained by the added plaintiffs from the original plaintiff. In the facts and circumstances of the case I cannot find my way but to agree with Mr. Hoque that the added plaintiffs who are petitioners herein have purchased the litigation and that the impugned kabala is not a forged but a genuine document having been executed by the plaintiff Chandra Narayan Sharmadhikari in favour of the defendant.

parties:
Nazrul Islam and another ----- Petitioners
Vs
Jahanara Hassan and another ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule issued at the instance of the defendants is directed against the judgment and order passed on 19.11.1990 by the Additional Assistant Judge Second Court, Dhaka allowing the plaintiffs prayer for amendment of the plaint of Title Suit No. 92 of 1990 (Originally Title Suit No. 160 of 1989 of the Local 3rd Court of Assistant Judge) 

 2. The opposite parties landlords brought the suit in the Third Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka for ejectment from certain premises of the petitioner No. 1 Nazrul Islam (Defendant No. 1) as the monthly tenant and the petitioner No. 2 Serajul Islam (Defendant No. 2) as sub-lessee, The suit had been valued at Taka 4,800.00 on the basis of the monthly rental of Taka 400.00. Before the defendants filed written statement the suit was transferred on 26.4.1990 by the District Judge to the Second Additional Court of the Assistant Judge. The Defendants filed written statement in the transferee court. Subsequently the plaintiffs filed a petition on 6.10.1990 praying for certain amendment in the plaint. The amendments were to the effect that the monthly rent of Taka 400.00 was enhanced to Tk. 600.00 as per a subsequent oral agreement, that in the cause title the suit was to be described as SCC suit instead of Title Suit and the valuation of the suit was to be raised in consequence of the enhanced rent to Taka 7,200.00 instead of Taka 4,800.00. The defendant filed a written objection taking the plea that the amendment would change the nature and character of the suit. After hearing the parties the learned Assistant Judge took the view that the amendment as proposed would not change the nature and character of the suit and accordingly allowed the prayer of the plaintiffs and fixed the suit for peremptory hearing. It is against this order that the defendants have obtained the instant Rule. 

 3. It is admitted on both sides that the original court has SCC powers but that the learned Additional Assistant Judge has no power to try SCC suits. Repeating the arguments advanced in the Court below Mr. Md. Azizul Huq the learned Advocate for the petitioners adds that the court could not allow an amendment ousting its own jurisdiction to try the suit and as such there has been a serious error of law resulting error in its decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. M Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate representing the other side submits that the suit for ejectment remains as before after the amendment is enough to indicate that there has been no change in the character of the plaint as well as the suit. Relying upon the decision in the case of Benisham Mohanlal Khetan Vs. Mohadeb Tukaram Borkar reported in AIR 1985 (Bombay) 462 he further submits that an amendment leading to ousting the jurisdiction of the court can be allowed. 

 4. It will appear that the suit was filed in a court which had SCC powers, but possibly due to some mistake in the cause title of the plaint and/or due to want of proper scrutiny by the office of the court the suit was registered in the Title file. The suit was subsequently transferred by the District Judge to a court which had/has no see powers. The mistake having been discovered by the plaintiffs the amendment petition was made for change into the file to which the suit would relate along with some other amendment on merit. 

 5. There is no question of change of nature and character of the suit by reason of the amendment on merit, that is, relating to the enhancement of the monthly rental under a subsequent oral agreement and the consequent enhancement of the valuation of the suit, and the learned Advocate for the petitioners does not have any such objection in relation thereto. He points out that the change in the nomenclature of the suit that is, from Title Suit to SCC suit, tantamount to a change in its nature and character. There is no dispute that an amendment of the plaint which would change the nature and character of the suit cannot be allowed. But the question is whether this change in the nomenclature of the suit would amount to such a change in its nature and character. It must be remembered that the plaint as it was filed for ejectment of a monthly tenant and in the proper court and as such it could not be but be registered as an see Suit. The mistake in registering the suit could not alter its nature and character. The amendment is prayed for merely to rectify the mistake by registering the suit in its proper file. It does not result in change of the character of the suit as such. In my view therefore the conversion of the suit from one file to another does not involve such a change in the nature and character of the suit as would bar an amendment of the plaint. 

 6. As to the question of ouster of jurisdiction there is no dispute that the transferee court has no see powers and that the effect of the amendment would certainly oust jurisdiction. The question is whether a court has power to allow such an amendment. The Division Bench decision cited on behalf of the opposite parties is exactly to the point In that ease an SCC Judge permitted an amendment of the plaint which had the effect of conversion of a suit on the basis of relationship of landlord and tenant into a suit based on title. After considering the only other processes open for being adopted in such matter, that is, either to return the plaint along with the amendment application outright, their Lordships held that the court had ample jurisdiction to allow the amendment and then to return the amended plaint to the plaintiffs for presentation to the proper court under Order 7 rule 10, CPC. I respectfully agree with the above decision.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Order No. 22 of 1971.
parties:
Munshi Ashadul Huq ------- Appellant, 
Vs. 
Nur Mohammad and ors  ------- Respondent.
full_judgment:
2. The petitioner-respondent No. 1 purchased the suit land from the decree-holder after the decree in the original title suit was passed but before the title appeal was filed. Thereafter the petitioner applied for being added as a respondent in the title appeal and by an order dated 11-2-69 the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the petitioner to be added as respondent No. 2 under Order 22 rule 10 C.P.C. The appeal was partly allowed and the decree-holder respondent was directed to deposit Taka 1400/- to the credit of the appellant and thereafter  the present execution proceeding was started. It may be noted in the connection that the suit out of which the present proceeding arose was for specific performance of a contract for re-conveyance. The petitioner offered to deposit the aforesaid sum of Taka 1400/- which was rejected but subsequently he was allowed by the learned Munsif deposit the same in the name of the original decree-holder.
